label: Chapter 7 · Part A
title: Common Objections I: “What Caused God?” and Other Misfires
tagline: Why the most popular objections miss the arguments they aim at
oneSentence: The best-known objections to First Cause arguments — “What caused God?”, “Maybe the universe is the uncaused cause”, “Why assume a beginning?”, “fallacy of composition”, “god of the gaps”, “a universe from nothing” — fail because they attack a caricature no major defender ever held, ignore the principled reasons the real arguments give, or quietly beg the question, so a serious critic has to engage the actual premises instead.
bigPicture:
After five proofs (chapters 1–5) and a long derivation of the divine attributes (chapter 6), Feser turns to the objections people actually raise. He has answered most of them already along the way, but he thinks a separate chapter is warranted for two reasons: there are some objections he has not yet addressed, and some of the weakest objections are so widespread — and so loudly repeated by the “New Atheist” writers (Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, Hitchens, Stenger, Krauss, Rosenberg, Grayling, Hawking and Mlodinow) — that they deserve a fresh, deeper look. This module covers the first half of that chapter: the objections aimed mainly at First Cause (cosmological) reasoning.

The unifying diagnosis is that almost every popular objection **misfires**: it is aimed at an argument nobody in the tradition ever gave. The flagship example is “If everything has a cause, then what caused God?” — an objection that presupposes the proofs start from the premise that *everything* has a cause, which none of them does. Feser devotes several pages to the history of this caricature, following the Thomist W. Norris Clarke in tracing it through Russell and the Mills back to Hume, who seems to have confused the rationalists’ talk of everything having a *sufficient reason* with the claim that everything has an *efficient cause distinct from itself*.

The remaining objections fall into recognizable families. Some nominate a rival stopping point (the universe, the Big Bang, the multiverse, quantum events, the laws of physics) while ignoring the criterion each proof uses to decide what can and cannot be a stopping point. Some deny that causal or explanatory principles hold universally, but rely on confusions (chance and indeterminism are not uncausedness) or on bad inferences (what we can *conceive* apart is not thereby *possible* apart). Some assume a temporal beginning or a linear series when the proofs concern a hierarchical, here-and-now series. Some misread technical terms — “necessary” as “true by definition”, “nothing” as a kind of exotic stuff. Some are true but irrelevant (the proofs don’t establish the Trinity). And the “god of the gaps” charge — which Feser calls the central conceit of the New Atheism — treats a metaphysical demonstration as if it were a rival scientific hypothesis.

This module matters enormously for the learner’s third goal, persuasion. In real conversations you will hear these objections far more often than any sophisticated criticism. Knowing *why* each one misfires, and being able to say so in a calm sentence or two, lets you redirect the conversation to where the genuine debate lies: whether the premises of the proofs — about act and potency, composition, essence and existence, and contingency — are true.
objectives: Explain the two independent reasons “If everything has a cause, what caused God?” fails: none of the proofs assumes everything has a cause, and each proof gives a principled reason why the First Cause could not have a cause.

Reconstruct W. Norris Clarke’s account of how the “everything has a cause” caricature entered the literature (Hume, the Mills, Russell, Hospers) through a confusion of efficient cause with sufficient reason.

Use each proof’s own criterion (potentiality, composition, essence–existence distinction, contingency) to show why the universe, Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events, or laws of physics cannot be the ultimate uncaused cause — and why the attempt would yield pantheism rather than atheism.
Distinguish chance and quantum indeterminism from uncausedness, and state three problems with Hume’s claim that we can conceive of an effect without a cause.
Explain why the proofs do not need a beginning of the universe, and why an endless stack of deeper physical laws would itself be a hierarchical series needing a first member.
Turn the fallacy-of-composition charge back on Hume and Grayling using the sticks, the mirrors, and Leibniz’s geometry books.
Distinguish logical, merely conditional, and metaphysical necessity, and use the distinction to rebut Kant’s and Grayling’s claim that the cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument.
Explain why the proofs are not “god of the gaps” reasoning, and why Krauss’s and Hawking–Mlodinow’s “universe from nothing” never actually starts from nothing.
Give a calm, one-sentence reply to each objection and then redirect the conversation to the real premises.

summary.heading: Why a chapter on objections at all
summary.body:
Most objections were already answered in earlier chapters, so Feser admits some overlap. A separate chapter is still warranted: some objections haven’t been addressed yet, and some very weak ones are so common — and so amplified by the New Atheist books of Harris, Dawkins, Dennett, Hitchens, Stenger, Hawking and Mlodinow, Krauss, Rosenberg, and Grayling — that they reveal pervasive misunderstanding and deserve a deeper look from new angles. Each section is headed by an objection in the critic’s own voice. This module covers the first run of them, aimed mainly at First Cause reasoning.

**How this chapter differs from the earlier ones.** Each of chapters 1–5 ended with objections aimed at that one proof. Chapter 7 steps back to objections against *natural theology* as a whole, meaning the project of reasoning to God without appealing to revelation. The book’s introduction had promised that the most common objections would turn out to be remarkably weak. This chapter is where Feser tries to deliver on that promise. The New Atheist books he has in view appeared between 2004 and 2013, and his footnotes cite them page by page, so his targets are specific rather than imagined.

A first-time reader should watch for three things. First, how often an objection turns out to be aimed at a premise the arguments never used. Second, how the *same* few principles from earlier chapters (act and potency, composition, essence and existence, contingency) keep answering objections that look quite different on the surface. Third, the difference between an objection that misfires and one that would be a genuine challenge. Feser is careful to say that genuine challenges are possible.
summary.plain: This chapter answers the objections people most often raise against arguments for God. Feser’s claim is that the most popular objections are also the weakest, because they attack versions of the arguments that nobody actually defends. Seeing why they fail clears the ground for the real discussion.
summary.takeaway: Chapter 7 exists because the weakest objections are also the most popular, and seeing why they fail clears the way for the real debate.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea here is that objections differ in kind.** Feser is not saying theism faces no serious difficulties. He is saying that the objections which *dominate* public discussion are of a peculiar type. They don’t dispute a premise the arguments actually use. They refute a different argument and then declare victory. This course calls that a *misfire*.

A medical comparison helps. Suppose a doctor diagnoses you from a blood test. One critic says, “Doctors are sometimes wrong, so this diagnosis is wrong.” Another says, “This particular test gives false positives after exercise, and you ran this morning.” The first objection sounds tough but touches nothing; the second engages the actual evidence. Chapter 7 argues that “What caused God?” and its cousins are like the first critic: forceful as rhetoric, idle as logic.

The course organizes Feser’s replies into a small diagnostic kit, set out in the `argument` section of this module:

- Is the objection aimed at a straw man (steps 1–2, 5)?
- Does it ignore the principled reason the arguments give for why some things need causes (steps 3, 7)?
- Does it confuse a chain through time with a hierarchy of present dependence (steps 4, 8)?
- Does it equivocate on “cause”, “necessary”, or “nothing” (steps 6, 11)?
- Does it beg the question by assuming only science explains (step 10)?
- Is it true but irrelevant (step 11)?

Almost everything in this module applies one of those tests.

**The nuance Feser adds.** He admits overlap with earlier chapters and promises new angles rather than repetition. And in answering the very first objection he concedes that a critic could legitimately challenge the premises, or argue that notions like pure actuality are incoherent (step 13). His polemical tone is aimed at a habit, repeating a caricature, not at the possibility of disagreement.

**The usual confusion.** Readers often take Feser’s confidence to mean he thinks the arguments are beyond criticism. On his own account they aren’t. What he denies is that the *popular* objections amount to that criticism.

checks.q: What does Feser mean in calling the most common objections weak?
options: They typically attack arguments no defender actually gives, so they never engage the real premises
They are raised by unintelligent people
Recent scientific discoveries have refuted them
They are too technical for ordinary readers
checks.explanation: The weakness is logical, not personal: the objections target a caricature. Feser explicitly notes that professionals raise them too.

checks.q: Which statement best reflects Feser’s attitude toward criticism of natural theology?
options: No criticism of the arguments could ever succeed
Only theists are qualified to criticize the arguments
Serious criticism is possible, but it must engage the actual premises and concepts
Criticism should be confined to scientific evidence
checks.explanation: He grants that a critic may challenge the premises or argue that the key concepts are incoherent. What he rejects is short-circuiting the arguments with a one-line retort.

summary.heading: “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”
summary.body:
Perhaps the most common objection of all, raised by amateurs and professionals and repeated across New Atheist literature. Feser finds two independent flaws.

**A straw man.** None of the book’s arguments has “everything has a cause” as a premise, so charges of self-contradiction or arbitrary exception miss.

**The arguments explain why God has no cause.** Their point is to show there must be something that *could not* have a cause because it lacks the feature that makes other things need one:

- **Aristotelian:** potentials can’t actualize themselves; the purely actual has none to actualize.
- **Neo-Platonic:** composites need something to unite their parts; the absolutely simple has no parts.
- **Thomistic:** a thing’s essence must have existence joined to it; that whose essence *is* existence needs nothing joined.
- **Rationalist:** contingent things could have been otherwise; a necessary being could not.

(A footnote sets aside the Augustinian proof, which isn’t a causal argument.) Restated in these terms, the question asks what actualized the potentials of what has none, or what assembled the parts of what has none — questions without sense. Feser grants the atheist may doubt the arguments succeed or try to expose hidden incoherence in these notions. That is a real objection, and it requires grappling with details; a single smug question cannot replace it.

**Why this matters.** The whole question turns on the difference between “everything has a cause” and “everything *of a certain kind* has a cause.” The first principle would indeed apply to God and generate a contradiction. The second applies only to things with the relevant feature, and the arguments conclude precisely that something lacks that feature. Feser adds that the objection fails for the same reason against the many other versions of the cosmological argument defended over the centuries, not just against his own five.
summary.plain: People often ask, “If everything needs a cause, what caused God?” Feser says the arguments never claimed that everything needs a cause. They claim that things of a certain sort (things that change, have parts, or might not have existed) need a cause, and they conclude that there must be something not of that sort. Asking what caused it is like asking who lent money to the one person who never borrowed any.
summary.takeaway: The arguments don’t exempt God from a rule; they conclude to the one thing that the rule, by its own terms, cannot apply to.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: an exception versus a conclusion.** The skeptic hears the theist saying, “Everything has a cause, except God.” That would be special pleading, like a referee who enforces the offside rule against every team but his own. Feser’s point is that the arguments have a different logical shape. They state what it is about a thing that makes it need a cause, and then show that something must *lack* that feature. Nothing is being exempted. The rule simply doesn’t reach that thing, by its own terms.

**A worked example, using the Aristotelian version.** Water in a kettle is cold but can become hot, so it has a potential. That potential doesn’t actualize itself; the flame does. But the flame’s heating depends, right now, on the gas burning, which depends on the gas’s chemical properties, which depend on its atoms continuing to exist with their structure. Each item actualizes something only because something else is actualizing *it*. The chain can end only in something that actualizes without being actualized, something with no potentials at all: pure actuality. Now ask, “What actualized pure actuality’s potentials?” It has none to actualize. The question isn’t unanswered; it is malformed, like asking for the name of a bachelor’s wife.

The other proofs have the same shape:

- A composite thing needs something to unite its parts, so the chain ends in the absolutely simple.
- A thing whose essence differs from its existence needs existence given to it, so the chain ends in what *is* existence.
- A contingent thing needs an outside explanation, so the chain ends in a necessary being.

This is step 3 of the misfire diagnosis, and it is what licenses step 5.

**Nuances.** Feser concedes two legitimate moves. A critic can doubt that the arguments really establish such a being, or argue that pure actuality, simplicity, and the rest are secretly incoherent (step 13). Feser also notes that the Augustinian proof isn’t a causal argument, so the objection doesn’t even appear relevant to it.

**The usual confusion.** People think the theist *defines* God as uncaused at the start. In fact uncausedness is derived at the end, which is why the objection has to engage the derivation and not a definition.

checks.q: According to the arguments Feser defends, ordinary things need a cause because:
options: everything whatsoever needs a cause
they have some specific feature, such as potentials needing actualization or parts needing combination
the universe had a beginning
God has decreed that everything be caused
checks.explanation: Each proof names a specific feature. That is why the conclusion (something lacking the feature) involves no exception.

checks.q: Why does Feser say “What caused God?” makes no sense when it is put in the arguments’ own terms?
options: Because God is too mysterious to be spoken of
Because the question would require a time before time
Because it asks what actualized potentials in something with no potentials, or united parts in something with no parts
Because causes are always physical
checks.explanation: Restated, the question presupposes that God has the very feature the argument showed he lacks. Mystery (A) and time (B) are not Feser’s points.

checks.q: Which of the following would Feser regard as a serious, non-misfiring response?
options: “If God needs no cause, the universe needs none either.”
“The argument assumes everything has a cause.”
“What caused God?”
“The idea of something purely actual hides a contradiction, and here is why.”
checks.explanation: Feser explicitly allows that a critic may argue these notions are incoherent; that engages the details. The others are the misfires he rebuts.

summary.heading: The straw man: the “basic cosmological argument”
summary.body:
The objection is popular because critics nearly always target a caricature. Feser’s examples span the spectrum: Dennett (New Atheist) says the argument’s simplest form is that everything has a cause, so the universe does; Nigel Warburton (popular introduction) says it traces a chain of prior causes back to a first one; Graham Priest (logician) motivates it with illnesses and car breakdowns having causes; Robin Le Poidevin (philosopher of religion) gives a three-step “basic cosmological argument” — whatever exists has a cause; nothing causes itself; the universe exists; so it has an external cause. Critics then ask what caused God, add that the argument assumes a beginning, and treat sophisticated versions as patches.

But not one major defender ever gave this argument — Feser lists some thirty, from Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, Avicenna, Maimonides, Aquinas, Scotus, and Leibniz to Garrigou-Lagrange, Swinburne, Koons, Pruss, Oderberg, and Craig. Le Poidevin concedes that “no-one has defended a cosmological argument of precisely this form,” yet calls it a stepping-stone.

Feser’s analogy: suppose ID theorists defined basic Darwinism as a monkey giving birth to a human, admitted no one holds it, but called it a stepping-stone. Darwinians would rightly protest that it frames all their real claims as salvage work on an absurdity.

Nor are defenders implicitly committed to it: none uses “everything has a cause” (some deny it); none assumes a beginning (only the kalām version tries to prove one); most make no claim about the universe as a whole.

**What the caricature gets wrong, in one line each.** It adds a universal causal premise the real arguments don’t use. It adds an assumption about a first moment of time the real arguments don’t need. And it makes the argument about the universe as a whole, when most versions can start from any single changing, composite, or contingent thing (in chapter 1, a stone or a cup of coffee).
summary.plain: Many books describe the First Cause argument as “everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause, which is God.” Feser shows that not one of the great defenders of the argument ever argued that way, and one critic even admits it. Starting a discussion with that version is like describing evolution as “a monkey gave birth to a human.” It makes the real view look silly before anyone has heard it.
summary.takeaway: No major defender ever gave the “basic cosmological argument”; treating it as the starting point distorts every later discussion.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: why a “harmless simplification” is not harmless.** Teachers simplify constantly, and that’s fine when the simplification keeps the logical skeleton. “Newton said force equals mass times acceleration” is a simplification. “Newton said heavy things fall faster” is a misstatement, and refuting it would refute nobody. Le Poidevin’s “basic cosmological argument” is the second kind. Compare its premises with the real ones:

- *Caricature:* everything that exists has a cause. *Real:* whatever has potentials actualized, is composite, has an essence distinct from its existence, or is contingent needs a cause.
- *Caricature:* trace causes back in time to the first one. *Real:* trace present dependence up to what sustains everything now; the past may have no beginning.
- *Caricature:* the universe as a whole needs a cause. *Real:* any single thing here and now is enough of a starting point.

Each change creates a weakness the real argument lacks: self-contradiction over God, dependence on cosmology, vulnerability to the composition charge. Those weaknesses then get blamed on Aquinas and Leibniz.

**The monkey analogy, slowly.** If ID theorists taught “basic Darwinism” as a monkey giving birth to a human, students would conclude that real Darwinism is a series of excuses for an absurdity. The damage isn’t just one bad argument; it is the *framing* of every later discussion. That is why Feser treats the stepping-stone defense as worse than a mere slip (steps 1, 2, 5).

**Nuances.** Craig defends the kalām argument, which does argue for a beginning. But he argues for it rather than assuming it, and only that one version cares about the question at all. Feser also singles out Le Poidevin as better informed than the other critics, which is what makes his use of the caricature so telling.

**The usual confusion.** People assume the sophisticated versions are later repairs to the simple one. Historically it’s the reverse. Aristotle’s and Aquinas’s arguments came first, and the “basic” version appears only in modern critics. The next section traces it back to Hume.

checks.q: Which writers does Feser quote as presenting the caricature?
options: Dennett, Warburton, Priest, and Le Poidevin
Aquinas, Leibniz, and Samuel Clarke
Anscombe, Gerson, and Oderberg
Plato, Aristotle, and Plotinus
checks.explanation: These four span New Atheism, popular philosophy, rigorous logic, and philosophy of religion. The other names are defenders or allies of the arguments.

checks.q: What does Feser say about the kalām cosmological argument in this context?
options: It is the only version that assumes everything has a cause
It is the only version even concerned to show the universe had a beginning, and it argues for that rather than assuming it
It is identical to Le Poidevin’s basic argument
It is the version the book defends

checks.q: A textbook opens: “The cosmological argument says everything has a cause, but then what caused God?” Which diagnostic test does this fail first?
options: True but irrelevant
Equivocation on “necessary”
Per se vs. per accidens confusion
Straw man: it targets a premise no defender uses
checks.explanation: The premise it attacks is absent from every major version, so the objection never reaches the real argument.

summary.heading: How the caricature spread: the Hume–Russell tradition
summary.body:
Critics learn about the argument from other critics, or read the caricature into Aquinas and Leibniz; repeated for generations, it became conventional wisdom even among specialists.

Feser follows W. Norris Clarke’s 1970 article on a “curious blind spot” in Anglo-American antitheism. Clarke found the caricature in mid-century textbooks, including John Hospers’ *An Introduction to Philosophical Analysis*, and suggested Russell’s *Why I Am Not a Christian* spread it; Russell got it from John Stuart Mill, who got it from James Mill; Hume’s *Dialogues* may be the first famous instance. Clarke notes that if anyone held “every being has a cause,” the refutation would be crushing — but its very ease should have raised suspicion, and no one in the tradition ever quotes a theist who holds it.

Hospers sneered that “many people” reach God by the argument and then forget it. Feser asks who they are, and turns the jibe around: the critics, having reached their preferred destination — dismissing Aristotle, Aquinas, and Leibniz wholesale — forget what those thinkers said. Clarke’s verdict: a tradition that misread its target at the start and has talked only to itself ever since.

**A practical lesson.** Clarke’s observation gives you a simple, courteous move in conversation: ask for a citation. “Which defender of the argument actually used the premise that everything has a cause?” If no one can be named, the objection is aimed at no one. This isn’t point-scoring. It is the same standard any historian or scientist applies before attributing a view to someone. It also explains *why* the objection feels so compelling to the people who raise it: they have heard it many times, from sources that seemed reliable.
summary.plain: How did such a misleading version become standard? Critics tended to learn about the argument from other critics rather than from its defenders, and the mistake was copied for generations. The Thomist philosopher W. Norris Clarke traced the chain back through Bertrand Russell and the Mills to David Hume. He noticed that none of these critics ever quoted a theist who actually argued that way.
summary.takeaway: The caricature survives because critics copy critics; Clarke found that none of them ever cites a theist who actually held it.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: how an error can live inside a tradition.** Mistakes about history often spread by citation rather than by checking. A familiar example is the myth that medieval people believed the earth was flat. It was popularized in the nineteenth century and then repeated in textbooks for generations, although educated medieval writers took the earth’s roundness for granted. Each author trusted the one before. Clarke’s diagnosis of the Hume–Russell tradition has the same structure. Hume attacked something like the caricature; the Mills and Russell repeated it; mid-century textbooks such as Hospers’ taught it; and later critics (Dennett, Warburton, Priest) absorbed it as common knowledge.

**Clarke’s two tests.**

1. *The ease of the refutation should arouse suspicion.* If the greatest philosophers of two millennia had really argued from “everything has a cause,” they would have noticed that the premise applies to God too. When a refutation is that easy, the charitable assumption is that you have misunderstood the view.
2. *Look for the citation.* Clarke found that nobody in the tradition quotes a theistic philosopher using the premise. Feser adds that the pattern has continued in the decades since Clarke wrote.

**Hospers turned around.** Hospers mocked people who use the argument to reach God and then forget the argument. Feser’s reply mirrors it: the critics use the caricature to reach the conclusion they want (that Aristotle, Aquinas, and Leibniz can be dismissed) and then forget what those thinkers actually said.

**How this feeds the formal argument.** This history is step 6 of the misfire diagnosis. Be careful about what it does and doesn’t do. It doesn’t *refute* the objection; steps 2 and 3 do that. It *explains* why a refuted objection remains so popular.

**The usual confusion.** People sometimes hear the genealogy as an insult to atheists. It is a claim about sources and habits, not motives. Feser’s charge is intellectual sloppiness, and he still grants that serious objections exist.

checks.q: Which chain of transmission does Clarke propose for the caricature?
options: Aquinas → Descartes → Kant → Russell
Hume → James Mill → John Stuart Mill → Russell → mid-century textbooks
Aristotle → Plotinus → Augustine → Hume
Dawkins → Dennett → Harris → Hitchens
checks.explanation: Clarke traces the line from Hume’s *Dialogues* through the Mills and Russell to textbooks like Hospers’.

checks.q: What role does the Hume–Russell genealogy play in Feser’s case?
options: It refutes “What caused God?” on its own
It shows that atheists argue in bad faith
It explains why the refuted objection is so widespread, while the refutation itself rests on what the arguments actually claim
It proves that the cosmological argument is sound
checks.explanation: The genealogy is explanatory, not refutational. Treating it as proof (A) or as a charge of bad faith (B) misreads its role.

summary.heading: Where the confusion began: two senses of “cause”
summary.body:
Clarke’s explanation of the origin: Hume misread Descartes and Spinoza. Descartes’ “preservation” argument in the Third Meditation implies that in some sense everything has a cause, but it still isn’t the straw man. It asks what keeps *Descartes* in existence, not what caused the universe; “everything has a cause” is not an explicit premise; and it makes no exception for God, whom Descartes calls self-caused.

What Descartes really means is close to the **principle of sufficient reason** (chapter 5): everything has an *explanation*. That differs from everything having a cause in the sense of an actualizer: all causes explain, but not all explanations are causes. PSR arguments make no exception for God — contingent things are explained by another, a necessary being by its own nature — so they contain no inconsistency.

Descartes and Spinoza blurred the two notions. Their word “cause” sounded like an **efficient cause distinct from its effect**, which God is said not to have. Hume fused the two claims and attributed the result to cosmological arguers generally, who indeed deny God has such a cause — hence the apparent contradiction. Clarke calls this target “a monster of their own fabrication,” a hybrid both Scholastics and Cartesians would reject. Hume had some excuse; his successors less. Feser treats assent to Clarke’s judgment as a test of competence and honesty, notes that Richard F. Clarke protested the same misrepresentation in 1889, and predicts the complaint will need repeating.

**The two senses side by side.**

- *Sense 1, sufficient reason:* whatever accounts for a thing’s existence. For a contingent thing it is something else; for a necessary being it is its own nature. Rationalists say everything has one, God included.
- *Sense 2, efficient cause distinct from its effect:* an outside producer. Theists of every school deny that God has one.

Neither sense produces a contradiction on its own. The contradiction appears only when the two are fused.
summary.plain: The mistake may have started with a word. Descartes and Spinoza said that everything, even God, has a “cause,” but they meant an *explanation*, and God’s explanation is his own nature. Hume heard “cause” in the ordinary sense of something outside a thing that produces it, and concluded that theists contradict themselves when they say nothing produced God.
summary.takeaway: Hume fused “everything has an explanation” with “everything has an outside cause,” producing a position no theist held.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: an explanation that isn’t a cause.** We usually explain something by pointing to what produced it. But some explanations point to a thing’s *nature* instead. Why do the interior angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to two right angles? Nothing *produced* that fact; it follows from what a triangle is. The rationalists thought God’s existence is explained in a comparable way: it follows from what God is. So God has a sufficient reason without having a producing cause. On Clarke’s reading, that is all “self-caused” meant for Descartes and Spinoza. It meant *self-explanatory*, not *self-producing*.

**How the fusion manufactures a contradiction.** Lay it out:

1. Rationalists: everything has a sufficient reason, God included.
2. Scholastics: God has no efficient cause distinct from himself.
3. Hume’s fusion: everything has an efficient cause distinct from itself.
4. Combine 3 with 2, and you get a contradiction.

But nobody asserts 3. Line 1 is true in sense 1; line 2 is true in sense 2. The contradiction exists only in the hybrid, the “monster” that Clarke says neither tradition would own.

**Descartes in particular.** His preservation argument asks what keeps *him* in existence from moment to moment. It isn’t about the universe; it doesn’t list “everything has a cause” as an explicit premise; and it makes no exception for God. So even the thinker who came closest to the premise isn’t caught by the objection.

**How this feeds the formal argument.** This is the content of step 6. It also shows why PSR-based arguments (the rationalist proof of chapter 5) are immune: they say absolutely everything has an explanation, with no exception at all.

**Nuances.** Clarke grants that Descartes’ replies to his critics are confusing and that Hume had some excuse; later critics, with modern scholarship at hand, have less. Richard F. Clarke’s complaint of 1889 shows the confusion was already entrenched by then.

**The usual confusion.** People think “self-caused” means God brought himself into being. That would be absurd, since he would have to exist before existing, and no one in either tradition meant it.

checks.q: On Clarke’s reading, what did Descartes and Spinoza mean in calling God “self-caused”?
options: That God’s existence is explained by his own nature
That God produced himself at the first moment of time
That God is caused by the universe
That God’s existence is a brute fact
checks.explanation: “Self-caused” meant self-explanatory, a sufficient reason lying in God’s own nature, not self-production.

checks.q: Which statement correctly relates causes and explanations?
options: Every explanation is a cause
Causes and explanations are unrelated
Every cause is an explanation, but not every explanation is a cause
Only physical causes explain
checks.explanation: A necessary being’s nature explains its existence without causing it. That asymmetry is what Hume overlooked.

checks.q: Why can’t “What caused God?” even get started against PSR-based arguments?
options: Because they assume the universe began
Because they deny that anything needs explaining
Because PSR applies only to physical objects
Because they hold that absolutely everything has an explanation, with God’s lying in his own nature, so there is no exception to expose
checks.explanation: No exception, no inconsistency. Whatever else one thinks of such arguments, the Humean objection has nothing to grab.

summary.heading: “Maybe the universe (or Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events, laws of physics) is the uncaused cause”
summary.body:
Found in Hume and in Dawkins, Dennett, Grayling, Krauss, Rosenberg, and Stenger, this also misses the point. The difference between God and everything else is principled, and the principle rules out these candidates:

- **Aristotelian:** the universe mixes act and potency; the Big Bang, each stage of a multiverse, and each quantum event (determinism aside) actualize potential; laws could have been otherwise, so are merely potential.
- **Neo-Platonic:** universe and multiverse are composite; laws and quantum events lack simplicity, their contingency revealing an essence–existence distinction.
- **Thomistic:** none has an essence identical with existence.
- **Rationalist:** all are contingent.

**Laws of nature** deserve special comment, their status being hotly disputed. If a law is a *statement of regularity*, it describes what needs explaining. If a *Platonic entity*, we must explain the world’s participation in it, and in these laws rather than others. If a *summary of how substances tend to behave* by nature (the Aristotelian view), it depends on those substances. On no view is it ultimate.

The atheist may reject these accounts, but merely *suggesting* the universe as terminus ignores the arguments. And success would yield **pantheism**, not atheism: a necessary, self-explanatory universe would be divine — acceptable to many Hindus, but not to Jews, Christians, Muslims, or atheists.

**The question to put to the objector.** Because the arguments supply a criterion, the burden is simple: show that your candidate lacks the relevant feature. Does the universe have no unrealized potentials? No parts? No gap between what it is and that it is? Could its laws not have been otherwise? Until one of those is shown, proposing the universe as the stopping point is a suggestion, not a reply.
summary.plain: Some people say that if God can exist without a cause, then so can the universe. Feser answers that the universe (along with the Big Bang, any multiverse, quantum events, and the laws of physics) has exactly the features that made us look for a cause: it changes, it has parts, and it could have been different. And if the universe really did exist necessarily and explain itself, it would be God under another name. That is pantheism, not atheism.
summary.takeaway: The universe, Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events, and laws all have the features that call for a cause — and a universe that lacked them would be God, pantheistically.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: why laws of nature can’t be the bottom level.** People say “the laws of physics explain everything” as if that ended the conversation. Feser asks what a law *is*, and whatever answer you give, the law turns out not to be ultimate. Try it with a humble law: water boils at 100°C at sea-level pressure.

1. *Regularity view:* the law just says that whenever water is heated to 100°C at that pressure, it boils. But that restates the pattern we wanted explained. Describing a pattern isn’t explaining it.
2. *Platonic view:* the law is an abstract entity that the world somehow conforms to. Then we must ask how this pot of water comes to “participate” in it, and why the world follows this law rather than one on which water boils at 90°C. The law needs explaining too.
3. *Aristotelian view:* the law summarizes how water tends to behave given its nature. Then the law is only as real as the water, and the water’s existence is precisely what is in question.

On every view, laws are not self-explaining foundations. That is step 7’s point about laws.

**Why indeterminism is irrelevant.** Someone may say quantum events are random, so nothing prior causes them. But a quantum event is still a potential being actualized, a system passing from one state to another, and that is what the Aristotelian criterion concerns. Whether the outcome was fixed in advance is a separate question.

**The pantheism twist.** Suppose the objector succeeds and the universe is necessary, uncaused, and self-explanatory. Then the universe has the attributes traditionally reserved for God. That is a theistic conclusion of a sort, pantheism, and it rules out atheism.

**Nuance.** Feser allows that an atheist may reject all three views of laws and all four proofs’ criteria. The point is that doing so takes argument.

**The usual confusion.** “The universe is everything, so there is nothing outside it to cause it.” That assumes only the physical exists, which is exactly what is in dispute. It begs the question (step 10).

checks.q: On the Aristotelian criterion, why can’t a quantum event be the uncaused cause, even if it is indeterministic?
options: Because quantum events are illusions
Because it still involves a potential being actualized, and indeterminism doesn’t change that
Because quantum events are deterministic after all
Because quantum events happen only in laboratories
checks.explanation: Feser says indeterminism is irrelevant: the event is still an actualization of potential.

checks.q: If a law of nature is just a statement that a regularity exists, what is the problem with treating it as the ultimate explanation?
options: It describes the pattern that needs explaining rather than explaining it
It makes the law a Platonic entity
It makes the law depend on God
It makes the universe composite
checks.explanation: A regularity statement redescribes the explanandum. The participation problem belongs to the Platonic view.

checks.q: A friend says, “Fine — the universe itself is necessary and self-explanatory.” What does Feser say follows?
options: Atheism is proved
The argument becomes merely probabilistic
The universe must have had a beginning
The universe would have divine attributes, so the view is pantheism, not atheism
checks.explanation: Even if the objection succeeded, it would identify God with the world rather than eliminate God.

summary.heading: “Not everything has a cause”: chance and quantum mechanics
summary.body:
Stenger cites chance, Dennett and Rosenberg cite quantum mechanics, Grayling cites Hume. Even setting aside that the proofs don’t use “everything has a cause”, none of this touches the causal principles they do use.

**Chance** presupposes non-chance causes. A farmer striking buried treasure is chance, but only because two causal lines — his plowing, someone’s burying — intersect. A boulder shattering another after an earthquake is chance, but it rests on tectonics, gravity, and solidity. No defender ever denied chance.

**Quantum mechanics** shows at most that some events lack a *deterministic* cause, and neither causality nor PSR demands determinism. Moreover, quantum events occur only given contingent quantum laws, merely potential until a universe obeying them is actualized — so the appeal misses the point or begs the question.

**Two ideas worth separating.** A *cause* is whatever brings something about. A *deterministic* cause is one that, given the circumstances, could only have produced exactly this result. Everyday life is full of causes that aren’t deterministic in any obvious way. Smoking causes cancer, but not in every smoker. A thrown die makes some face land up, but not a predictable one. Nobody concludes that the cancer or the die’s result is uncaused. The principles the proofs rely on (that a potential is actualized only by something actual, and that things have explanations) say nothing about determinism. So even if physics shows that the deepest causes are probabilistic, the principles are untouched.

The chance examples make a parallel point. Chance isn’t an alternative to causation; it is a pattern among causes, in which independent lines meet without anyone planning the meeting.
summary.plain: Some critics say chance events or quantum physics prove that things can happen without causes. Feser replies that chance is just what we call it when two unrelated chains of causes happen to meet, like a farmer’s plow hitting buried treasure. And quantum physics shows at most that some causes don’t fix a single outcome in advance, not that events happen with no cause at all.
summary.takeaway: Chance and indeterminism are ways causes operate, not evidence that things happen without causes.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: unpredictable is not the same as uncaused.** Take a single uranium-238 nucleus. Physics can’t tell you when it will decay. It can only tell you that half of a large sample will decay in about 4.5 billion years. Does that mean the decay has no cause? Look at what’s doing the work. A uranium nucleus decays and a lead nucleus doesn’t, and uranium decays at *its* characteristic rate, not at carbon-14’s. The nature of the nucleus and the laws of quantum mechanics fix the probabilities. The decay is a potential in the nucleus being actualized: indeterministically, but not out of nowhere.

Feser makes two points (steps 9 and 10):

1. *Wrong target.* The principle of causality and PSR require a cause or explanation, not a deterministic one. Showing that some causes are indeterministic doesn’t touch them.
2. *A presupposed framework.* Quantum events happen only within the laws of quantum mechanics and in physical systems governed by them. Those laws are contingent, since they could have been otherwise, and they are merely potential until there is a universe that follows them. So appealing to quantum events as the uncaused foundation either misses the point or begs the question, because they belong to the very reality whose existence is being explained.

**The chance cases, slowly.** The farmer didn’t intend to find treasure, and the person who buried it didn’t intend it to be found. The discovery was nobody’s plan, yet each line was thoroughly causal. The same holds for the boulders after an earthquake: which boulder hits which is chance, but tectonics, gravity, and solid rock are not. Chance *requires* regular, non-chance causes in the background.

**Nuance.** Feser doesn’t need to take sides among the interpretations of quantum mechanics. His argument works even on the standard indeterministic reading.

**The usual confusion.** People slide from “we can’t predict it” to “nothing causes it.” Prediction concerns our knowledge; causation concerns what brings the event about.

checks.q: Why does Feser say Stenger’s appeal to chance attacks a straw man?
options: Because Stenger misdescribes quantum physics
Because chance events are illusions
Because chance applies only to games
Because no defender of the cosmological argument denies that chance events occur
checks.explanation: Defenders never denied chance; they deny that chance excludes causation, since it presupposes it.

checks.q: A student says, “Nobody can predict when a nucleus will decay, so the decay is uncaused.” What is the key mistake?
options: Confusing unpredictability or indeterminism with the absence of any cause
Assuming the nucleus is composite
Committing the fallacy of composition
Confusing logical with metaphysical necessity
checks.explanation: The nucleus’s nature and the quantum laws fix the probabilities; an indeterministic cause is still a cause.

summary.heading: The Humean objection: three problems
summary.body:
Grayling treats Hume’s claim that effects can be conceived apart from causes as decisive. Feser gives three reasons it isn’t.

1. **Special pleading.** No working scientist would accept that a phenomenon under study might have no cause; why accept it here? And, as Lloyd Gerson notes, the cosmological argument *is* an explanation, so “maybe there’s no explanation” gives no reason to reject it.
2. **Conceivability isn’t possibility.** One can conceive of a triangle without conceiving it as trilateral, or of a man without his height; neither could exist that way.
3. **Anscombe: underdescription.** What makes Hume’s imagined sudden appearance an *uncaused* coming-to-be rather than one with an unseen cause, or a teleportation? Settling that seems to require causation — e.g., distinguishing a generating from a transporting cause.

Earlier chapters treat these objections more fully.

**Why the special-pleading point has teeth.** Science works by refusing to accept “maybe there’s no explanation” for anything it studies. If a lab result looked uncaused, researchers would keep looking rather than publish a paper announcing an uncaused event. A critic who finds brute facts acceptable only for the existence of the universe owes an account of why that one case is different. Gerson’s point strengthens this. The cosmological argument isn’t waiting for an explanation; it *offers* one. To reject it, the critic needs a positive reason, not just the bare possibility that no explanation exists.

**Why conceiving isn’t enough.** Imagination is selective. We can attend to one feature of a thing while ignoring others. That tells us about our attention, not about which features the thing could exist without.
summary.plain: Hume argued that because we can imagine something popping into existence with no cause, it could really happen. Feser gives three replies. First, scientists never accept “maybe it has no cause” anywhere else. Second, imagining one thing without thinking of another doesn’t show they can come apart: you can think of a triangle without thinking “three-sided,” but no triangle lacks three sides. Third, as the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe showed, you can’t even say what makes your imagined event *uncaused* without bringing causes back in.
summary.takeaway: Being able to imagine an effect without its cause shows nothing about what can exist, and the imagined scene can’t even be described without causation.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: Anscombe’s underdescription argument.** Try Hume’s experiment honestly. Picture your desk at noon, empty. Then picture it a second later with a rabbit on it. You have “conceived” something appearing. But which of these have you conceived?

1. A rabbit coming into existence with no cause.
2. A rabbit coming into existence from a cause you can’t see.
3. An existing rabbit transported to the desk by some unusual means (teleportation, say).

The picture is the same in all three. Nothing in the imagery settles which it is, so you haven’t yet conceived what Hume needs, namely (1) in particular. To pick out (1), you have to add something. The natural way to tell “came into being” from “was moved here” is that the first involves a *generating* cause and the second a *transporting* cause, and that reintroduces causation. Strip out all causal notions, and the difference between (1) and (3) vanishes. So the scenario can’t be described the way Hume needs without undermining his point.

**The triangle point, sharpened.** Hume needs more than “I can think of an effect without thinking of its cause.” He needs “I can think of an effect *together with the absence* of any cause.” The triangle case shows the gap. Thinking of a triangle without thinking of its three sides is easy; thinking of a triangle *that lacks* three sides is impossible. Leaving something out of your thought is not the same as thinking it isn’t there.

**How this feeds the formal argument.** All three points belong to step 9 (denials of causal principles rest on bad inference). The special-pleading point also belongs to step 10.

**Nuance.** Feser doesn’t claim that conceivability is never evidence of possibility. His claim is narrower: this inference, from this act of imagining, doesn’t establish that uncaused beginnings are possible. He refers readers to earlier chapters for a fuller treatment.

**The usual confusion.** People think Hume showed that the causal principle is merely a habit of expectation. Even if Hume’s psychology is granted, the argument from conceivability doesn’t show the principle is false.

checks.q: Which point does Feser credit to Lloyd Gerson?
options: That Hume’s scenario is underdescribed
That the cosmological argument is itself a proposed explanation, so “maybe there’s no explanation” is no reason to reject it
That chance presupposes causes
That laws of nature summarize the natures of substances
checks.explanation: Underdescription is Anscombe’s point; the laws view is Oderberg’s. Gerson shifts the burden onto the critic.

checks.q: According to the sharpened version of the triangle point, what does Hume’s argument need?
options: To conceive of an effect while ignoring its cause
To conceive of a cause without its effect
To prove that effects exist
To conceive of an effect together with the absence of any cause, which the triangle case shows is a different thing
checks.explanation: Omitting something from a thought differs from thinking it absent. Hume shows only the first.

checks.q: In Anscombe’s argument, what distinguishes coming into being from being transported?
options: The speed of the appearance
Whether an observer is present
A generating cause versus a transporting cause
Whether the object is large or small
checks.explanation: The distinction is itself causal, so imagining an uncaused coming-to-be requires the concept of cause it was meant to exclude.

summary.heading: “Why assume a beginning, or that the regress must end?”
summary.body:
Rosenberg and Krauss suggest a beginningless multiverse, with our Big Bang branching from a prior universe, removes the need for God; Krauss, citing Feynman, adds there might be endless deeper layers of physical law.

- The arguments don’t concern a beginning. Even a beginningless universe or multiverse would need a divine cause to sustain it and to explain why it exists at all.
- Laws cannot be ultimate explanations, however many layers.
- Stacked laws, each holding only as a special case of a deeper one, would form a **hierarchical series** of the chapter 1 kind, which must have a first member imparting causal power without deriving it. The New Atheists never address this.

**Two kinds of chain, again.** The distinction from chapter 1 does all the work here. In a *temporal* chain (grandparents, parents, children), earlier members can die off and later ones carry on, and nothing obviously rules out such a chain having no first member. In a *hierarchical* chain (a hand pushing a stick pushing a stone), every member acts only while the one above it acts; take away the top and everything stops at once. Chapter 1 argued that the things around us depend in the second way: a cup of coffee exists at this moment only because deeper levels of reality are, at this moment, keeping it in existence. The question “did the universe have a beginning?” concerns the first kind of chain. The proofs concern the second. That is why Feser can grant, for the sake of argument, an infinite past or a beginningless multiverse without any damage to his case.
summary.plain: Critics ask why we should think the universe had a beginning, and point to theories of an endless multiverse. Feser’s answer is that his arguments never needed a beginning. They ask what keeps things in existence right now, and even an endless chain of universes would need that. In the same way, an endless stack of deeper and deeper physical laws would still be a chain in which each layer borrows its power from the next, so there must be a source that doesn’t borrow.
summary.takeaway: The proofs don’t care whether time began; they care what keeps things existing and acting now — and endless layers of law would be a hierarchy needing a top.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: why an endless stack of laws is a hierarchy, not a timeline.** Krauss, following Feynman, imagines physicists probing deeper and deeper layers of law until they get bored. Take a real example of layering. Kepler’s laws of planetary motion hold because (approximately) Newton’s law of gravitation holds. Newton’s law holds as an approximation of general relativity. And physicists expect general relativity to hold as a special case of some deeper theory. The relation between the layers isn’t “earlier and later.” It is “this holds *because* that holds,” right now and all at once. Each layer has its force only derivatively, from the layer beneath.

That is exactly the structure of a per se series (step 4). Chapter 1 showed that such a series needs a first member no matter how long it is. The number of members is irrelevant; what matters is that every member has only borrowed power. An infinitely long series of borrowers still contains no lender. So “layers all the way down” doesn’t escape the argument. It describes one more hierarchy that needs something with underived causal power (step 8).

Notice too that “until we get bored” is about *our investigation*, not about reality. Perhaps experiments will never reach the bottom layer. That wouldn’t show there is no first member. It would only show that physics can’t find it, which the proofs never expected it to.

**Nuances.** Feser’s reply has three parts: beginnings are irrelevant; laws can’t be ultimate however many there are; and layered laws form a hierarchy. He also says the New Atheists never address this kind of argument at all.

**The usual confusion.** “First cause” sounds like “earliest cause,” so people picture the Big Bang. In the proofs, “first” means *underived*: the source whose causal power isn’t borrowed, not the first thing in time. Think of it as the top of a hierarchy rather than the front of a queue.

checks.q: Rather than whether the universe had a beginning, what does Feser say the book’s arguments are concerned with?
options: What sustains things in existence, and explains why they exist at all, whether or not they began
Whether the universe is finite in size
Whether time is real
Whether the Big Bang was caused by a prior universe
checks.explanation: Even a beginningless universe or multiverse would need a sustaining cause and an explanation of its existence.

checks.q: In the per se sense, “first cause” means:
options: the earliest event in history
the largest cause
the cause that acted at the Big Bang
the member of the series whose causal power is underived
checks.explanation: “First” refers to rank in a hierarchy of dependence, not to position in time.

checks.q: A physicist says, “Maybe there’s no bottom layer of physical law; we’ll just keep finding deeper ones.” Which reply is Feser’s?
options: Physics will certainly find the bottom layer
Physical laws are illusions
Layers in which each holds only because a deeper one does form a hierarchical series, which needs a first member with underived power however many layers there are
Deeper laws would contradict the Big Bang
checks.explanation: The length of a per se series is irrelevant. Derivative members never add up to an underived source.

summary.heading: “First Cause arguments commit a fallacy of composition”
summary.body:
The book’s arguments needn’t make any claim about the universe as a whole, and chapter 5 showed that the rationalist’s possible inference from contingent parts to a contingent whole isn’t fallacious.

Grayling, after Hume, says that once each member of a collection is explained, nothing is left over. Feser disagrees, recalling:

- **Sticks:** an infinite series of sticks, none able to move by itself individually or collectively, still needs an outside mover.
- **Mirrors:** an infinite row reflecting a face still needs a real face.
- **Leibniz’s geometry books:** endless copying from earlier copies never explains why the series has *this* content.

So Hume and Grayling commit the fallacy: explaining each member by its neighbor doesn’t explain why there is motion, an image, or geometrical content in the series at all.

**What the fallacy is, and isn’t.** A fallacy of composition assumes that because every part has a property, the whole must have it: every brick is light, so the wall is light. But some properties *do* carry over. If every Lego brick in a model is red, the model is red. Chapter 5 argued that contingency behaves like color, not weight, since a collection of contingent things is if anything *more* obviously contingent than any one of them.

Two separate questions are in play here. One: is the whole series contingent? (That was chapter 5’s issue.) Two: once each member is explained by another, is anything left to explain? Grayling says no. Feser says yes, and his examples are designed to show that the “nothing left over” claim is itself the faulty part-to-whole inference. Remember, finally, that the arguments don’t need any premise about the universe as a whole. They can start from a single thing existing here and now.
summary.plain: Critics say it is a logical mistake to ask for an explanation of a whole series once each member has been explained by the one before it. Feser replies with examples. An endless line of sticks, each pushing the next, still needs something to start the pushing. An endless row of mirrors still needs a real face to reflect. Explaining each member by its neighbor doesn’t explain the whole, so the mistake is actually the critic’s.
summary.takeaway: Explaining each member of a series by its neighbor does not explain the series; the critic, not the theist, commits the fallacy.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: why “each member is explained” doesn’t mean “the series is explained.”** Picture a freight train of boxcars rolling along a track. Car 1 moves because car 2 pulls it; car 2 moves because car 3 pulls it; and so on. Now suppose, as the critic allows, that the train is infinitely long and has no locomotive. For every car there is a true answer to “why is it moving?”: the next car pulls it. Yet something is obviously wrong. None of the cars can move anything on its own; each only passes along motion it receives. With no engine, there is no motion to pass along. Explaining every car by the next one leaves unexplained why there is any motion at all.

Feser’s three examples have the same shape:

- **Sticks:** no stick can move by itself, individually or collectively.
- **Mirrors:** no mirror generates an image; it only reflects one.
- **Geometry books:** each copy owes its content to an earlier copy, which leaves open why the series contains geometry rather than a cookbook.

The critic’s inference runs: *for each n, member n is explained by member n+1; therefore the whole series is explained.* That moves from what is true of each part to what is true of the whole. It is a composition inference, and here a bad one. So the charge rebounds on the critic.

**How it feeds the formal argument.** This applies step 4 (the relevant regress is hierarchical, made of members with only derived power) and step 8 (confusing that with a chain of self-sufficient links). It also depends on step 2: most versions don’t reason from the universe as a whole anyway.

**Nuance.** The sticks and mirrors illustrate hierarchical series from chapter 1. Leibniz’s books come from his own rationalist argument, and Feser uses them to show that the same point holds for explanation in general.

**The usual confusion.** People think theists argue “each part is contingent, so the whole is.” That is at most one possible version of one proof, and even it isn’t fallacious. The core arguments start from any single dependent thing.

checks.q: Which example comes from Leibniz?
options: The infinite series of copied geometry books
The farmer and the buried treasure
The hand, stick, and stone
The monkey giving birth to a human
checks.explanation: Leibniz used the endlessly copied geometry books in “On the Ultimate Origination of Things.”

checks.q: Why does Feser say it is Hume and Grayling who commit the fallacy of composition?
options: Because they claim the universe is red
Because they infer, from each member’s being explained by another, that the whole series is explained
Because they deny that the universe has parts
Because they reason from the whole to the parts
checks.explanation: The move from “each is explained” to “the whole is explained” is the invalid part-to-whole step.

checks.q: A friend says, “Every event in history was caused by a previous event, so history as a whole needs no further explanation.” Which example best exposes the mistake?
options: The triangle and the trilateral
The farmer’s treasure
The monkey analogy
The row of mirrors: explaining each image by the next mirror never explains where the face came from
checks.explanation: The mirrors show that passing something along never accounts for its being there at all.

summary.heading: “Even if there were a first cause, why think it is God?”
summary.body:
Grayling, Dawkins, and Krauss assert there’s no reason to ascribe omnipotence, omniscience, or goodness to a first cause. Feser calls this as inept as “What caused God?” Defenders have given abundant arguments: Aquinas spends about a hundred double-column pages of the *Summa Theologiae* (right after the Five Ways) on simplicity, goodness, infinity, immutability, unity, knowledge, life, will, and power, and about two hundred pages of *Summa Contra Gentiles* book 1, with more in *De potentia* and *De veritate*; Samuel Clarke’s *Demonstration of the Being and Attributes of God* argues for infinity, omnipresence, unity, intelligence, free choice, power, wisdom, and goodness; Aristotle, Plotinus, Avicenna, Scotus, and Leibniz likewise. The New Atheists seem unaware of these arguments. And chapters 1–6 of this book argue for the attributes in detail. The objection is groundless.

**What such derivations look like.** The book’s introduction describes every proof as having two stages. The first establishes something fitting a key description, such as an uncaused cause or a purely actual actualizer. The second shows that whatever fits that description must have the divine attributes. To give the flavor of stage two from chapter 6: change is the actualization of potential, so something with no potential cannot change, which makes it *immutable*. And for there to be two things of the same kind, they must differ in something, which requires potentiality, so there can be only one purely actual being: *unity*. Omnipotence, omniscience, and goodness get longer treatments in the second half of chapter 6. The objection treats the second stage as if it didn’t exist.
summary.plain: Some critics say that even if there is a first cause, there’s no reason to think it is all-powerful, all-knowing, or good. Feser points out that defenders have written hundreds of pages deriving exactly those attributes. Aquinas alone devotes about three hundred pages to them across two works, and Feser’s own book does the same, especially in chapter 6. The critics simply don’t engage those arguments.
summary.takeaway: The move from first cause to God is not a leap but a long, well-documented argument that the critics never engage.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: why the attributes are consequences, not additions.** The critic imagines the argument reaching a thin, featureless “first cause,” to which the theist then bolts on omnipotence, omniscience, and goodness because the Bible says so. But the first cause the proofs arrive at is not thin. It is described by what it lacks (no potentiality, no parts, no distinction of essence and existence), and each lack has consequences.

Work one through slowly. *Pure actuality means no unrealized potential.* Change is the actualization of potential, so pure actuality cannot change: that is immutability. Time is bound up with change, so what cannot change is not in time: eternity. Matter always involves potential, since it can take on other forms, so what has no potential isn’t material: immateriality. And two purely actual beings would have to differ in something, meaning that one has a feature the other lacks. That is a limitation, and so a potentiality, which gives unity. None of these is added from outside; each unpacks what “purely actual” already means. (See ch6a and ch6b for the full arguments, including the longer routes to power, knowledge, and goodness.)

**The historical record.** Feser’s point in this section is partly historical. The sources include Aquinas (roughly a hundred double-column pages in the *Summa Theologiae* and two hundred in the *Summa Contra Gentiles*, plus other works), Samuel Clarke, Aristotle, Plotinus, Avicenna, Scotus, and Leibniz. The critics’ claim that there is no reason whatsoever can only mean they haven’t looked.

**How it feeds the formal argument.** This is part of step 11: an objection that ignores the arguments actually given doesn’t touch the conclusion.

**The usual confusion.** People think the arguments at best prove a vague “something,” a cosmic force or an impersonal energy. The derivations are meant to rule that out. Whatever is purely actual, simple, and self-existent turns out to have intellect, will, power, and goodness (chapter 6).

checks.q: According to Feser, what do Dawkins, Grayling, and Krauss fail to do regarding the divine attributes?
options: Respond to any of the many historical arguments for them
Accept that a first cause exists
Read Hume
Consider the multiverse
checks.explanation: Feser says they seem unaware that arguments by Aquinas, Samuel Clarke, and others even exist.

checks.q: Why does immutability follow from pure actuality?
options: Because God has decided never to change
Because change is the actualization of potential, and what is purely actual has no potential to actualize
Because the universe is immutable
Because simplicity implies eternity
checks.explanation: This derivation appears in chapter 6: no potential means no change.

summary.heading: “It wouldn’t prove prophets, the Bible, or the Trinity”
summary.body:
True, but irrelevant. The arguments aim at one tenet shared by many religions — a cause of the world that is one, simple, immaterial, eternal, immutable, omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good. If they succeed, atheism is false and the open question is which theism to adopt (philosophical theism, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, or another), which needs further inquiry. Not answering every question about God is not answering none — as special relativity isn’t refuted by its silence on evolution, nor quantum mechanics by leaving engineering questions open.

**Natural versus revealed theology.** Philosophers distinguish what can be known about God by reason alone (natural theology) from what could be known only if God revealed it (revealed theology). The Trinity, the inspiration of Scripture, and the calling of prophets belong to the second category; Feser’s arguments belong entirely to the first. His introduction says as much. The real debate, he says there, is not between atheism and theism but between different kinds of theists (Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, purely philosophical theists), and the book deliberately doesn’t enter that further debate. The end of chapter 6 discusses what a miracle is, which bears on whether revelation is even possible, but whether any revelation has actually occurred lies outside the book.

Notice, too, how much the arguments do claim to establish. They conclude not to a vague force but to a cause of the world that is one, simple, immaterial, eternal, immutable, all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good. So the objection’s premise is correct. Only its implied conclusion, that the arguments are therefore pointless or have failed, is wrong.
summary.plain: Another complaint is that even an all-powerful, all-knowing, good God wouldn’t prove the Bible, the prophets, or the Trinity. Feser agrees, and says it doesn’t matter. The arguments aim to show that God exists, which already rules out atheism. Which religion, if any, is true is a further question. A theory isn’t refuted because it doesn’t answer every question.
summary.takeaway: Proving God’s existence is not the same as proving a particular religion, and failing to do the second doesn’t undo the first.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: the logic of partial results.** An argument can succeed completely at what it attempts while leaving other questions open. A detective who proves that someone was in the room when the vase broke has refuted the claim that no one was there, even before identifying who. A test that proves an infection is bacterial hasn’t named the bacterium, but it has ruled out a virus. In the same way, if the arguments prove there is a cause of the world that is one, simple, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good, they have refuted atheism, even though they haven’t settled whether Christianity, Judaism, Islam, or philosophical theism is correct.

Feser’s analogies make the same point from science. No one rejects special relativity because it is silent about evolution, or quantum mechanics because it doesn’t answer every engineering question. Every theory has a domain, and criticizing it for not going beyond that domain is a category mistake.

**How much is actually established.** Don’t underestimate stage two. The God of these arguments isn’t a vague “higher power.” The attributes rule out polytheism (by unity) and, as chapter 6 argues, pantheism and deism as well, since God is distinct from the changing world and sustains it at every moment. They also rule out any merely finite designer. That is already the core of classical theism, shared by the great monotheistic traditions.

**How it feeds the formal argument.** This is the “true but irrelevant” test in step 11.

**The usual confusion.** Believers and skeptics alike sometimes assume that natural theology is disguised apologetics for one religion, and so they judge it by whether it proves that religion. Feser’s project is narrower and, in a sense, prior: to establish the common ground from which the further questions can be argued.

checks.q: How does Feser characterize the objection that the arguments don’t prove the Trinity?
options: False and dangerous
A fallacy of composition
True but completely irrelevant
A straw man of Christian doctrine
checks.explanation: He agrees with the statement but denies it bears on whether the arguments succeed.

checks.q: Which analogy does Feser use for this objection?
options: The monkey giving birth to a human
Rejecting special relativity because it says nothing about evolution
The farmer’s buried treasure
Leibniz’s geometry books
checks.explanation: A theory isn’t refuted by its silence on questions outside its domain.

summary.heading: “The cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument”
summary.body:
Kant’s objection, repeated by Grayling, targets Descartes’ ontological argument (existence is a perfection, so a supremely perfect being must exist), on which God would exist *by definition*. Since the cosmological argument ends with a necessary being, Kant says it relies on that argument, which fails because existence is not a perfection.

**Reply.** Aquinas and most Thomists reject the ontological argument but defend the cosmological, so dependence can’t just be asserted. Nor are they inconsistent: as chapter 6 showed, the necessity they ascribe to God isn’t definitional, and Kant’s charge works only if it is.

**Grayling’s refinement.** A defender might call God *metaphysically* rather than *logically* necessary — a stopping point grounding contingent existence. But that, says Grayling, makes God merely a necessary *condition* of the world, not something that couldn’t fail to exist.

**Reply: a false dichotomy.** Metaphysical necessity can be unconditional without being logical. For the Aristotelian, contingency comes from mixing act and potency, so pure actuality exists necessarily. For the Neo-Platonist, it comes from composition, so the absolutely simple is necessary. For the Thomist, the first cause is necessary because its essence *is* existence, so nothing must be added to it. A footnote insists on “is” rather than “includes”, which would imply composition.

**The direction of reasoning.** The ontological argument reasons *downward* from a concept to existence: define God, then infer that he exists. The cosmological argument reasons *upward* from things we observe (change, composite things, contingent things) to what they depend on, and only then asks what that source must be like. Its conclusion that the source exists necessarily is a discovery about the source’s nature, not a definition assumed at the start. That is why Aquinas could reject the one argument and defend the other.
summary.plain: Kant claimed that the First Cause argument secretly relies on a different argument, the “ontological” argument, which tries to prove God exists by definition. Feser replies that when these arguments call God “necessary,” they don’t mean he exists by definition. They mean there is nothing in God that could fail: no unused potential, no parts that could come apart, and no gap between what he is and that he is.
summary.takeaway: The cosmological argument’s necessary being is necessary because of what it is (no potential, no parts, essence identical with existence), not because of a definition.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: three kinds of necessity.** Everything here turns on keeping them apart.

1. **Logical (definitional) necessity.** “2 + 2 = 4” and “bachelors are unmarried” are true because of what the terms mean; denying them is self-contradictory. The ontological argument claims that God’s existence is like this.
2. **Conditional (relative) necessity.** Oxygen is necessary *for this fire*. That says nothing about whether oxygen had to exist; it is necessary only relative to something else. Grayling says metaphysical necessity collapses into this kind.
3. **Metaphysical (real, unconditional) necessity.** Think about why ordinary things can cease to exist. A candle can burn away because it has parts that can separate and potentials that can be realized in other ways. A person can die because the matter composing him can become something else. Now imagine something with no parts and no potentials at all. There is nothing in it that could come apart, and no potential for being otherwise, including a potential for not existing. Its necessity comes from what it is, not from the definition of a word or from its relation to something else.

Feser gives three routes to (3). *Aristotelian:* contingency comes from mixing act and potency, so pure act exists necessarily. *Neo-Platonic:* contingency comes from composition, so the absolutely simple is necessary. *Thomistic:* contingency comes from existence having to be added to an essence, so what *is* existence is necessary. Grayling’s choice between (1) and (2) simply leaves out (3). That makes it a false dichotomy (step 11).

**Kant’s point, slowly.** Kant reasoned like this: the cosmological argument ends with a necessary being; the only necessary being would be one whose existence follows from its concept; that is the ontological argument; so the cosmological argument depends on it. Feser denies the second premise. Only because of this is Aquinas’s position (rejecting the ontological argument while accepting the cosmological) consistent.

**Nuance.** In a footnote, Feser says God’s essence *is* existence rather than “including” it, since inclusion suggests parts.

**The usual confusion.** People take “necessary being” to mean a being we can’t imagine not existing. The claim concerns the being’s nature, not our powers of imagination.

checks.q: Which thinker does Feser use as a counterexample to Kant’s claim of dependence?
options: Descartes
Anselm
Aquinas, who rejected the ontological argument but defended the cosmological
Spinoza
checks.explanation: Aquinas and most Thomists hold exactly the combination Kant says is impossible, and they hold it consistently.

checks.q: Grayling says metaphysical necessity is merely conditional. Why does Feser call this a false dichotomy?
options: Because conditional and logical necessity are the same
Because there is a third option: unconditional necessity grounded in a thing’s nature, such as pure actuality, simplicity, or essence identical with existence
Because God is only logically necessary
Because necessity is a purely linguistic notion
checks.explanation: The three metaphysical accounts give necessity that is neither definitional nor merely relative.

checks.q: Which of these is an example of merely conditional necessity?
options: Oxygen’s being necessary for a fire
Two plus two equaling four
Pure actuality’s existing
A bachelor’s being unmarried
checks.explanation: Oxygen is necessary only relative to the fire. B and D are logical necessities; C is metaphysical.

summary.heading: “God of the gaps”
summary.body:
The charge that God is invoked to fill a gap science has filled or will fill is, Feser says, the central conceit of the whole New Atheism: all genuine explanation is scientific, so God is at best a poor quasi-scientific hypothesis. Hitchens invokes Ockham’s razor; Dawkins thinks a Big Bang singularity or unknown physical concept more economical; Harris says nobody knows how the universe came to be; Krauss, Hawking, and Mlodinow think science has (nearly) explained it — Hawking and Mlodinow claiming that because of a law like gravity, “the universe can and will create itself from nothing.”

The **first** of two problems: this misses the point or begs the question.

- **Not gap-filling.** A god-of-the-gaps account allows that a natural explanation might in principle be correct and claims only greater probability. The book’s arguments are strict metaphysical demonstrations claiming no other explanation is possible in principle; they are not judged by parsimony or fit with current theory.
- **Metaphysical starting points.** They start from what any empirical theory presupposes: actualization of potential, composition, essence joined to existence, contingency. Insisting only science can explain assumes these arguments wrong without showing it.

**What a real gap argument looks like.** Historically, some thinkers did appeal to God to explain specific physical puzzles. Newton, for example, suggested that God might occasionally adjust the planets’ orbits to keep the solar system stable, a role that later physics made unnecessary.
