Arguments like that really are vulnerable to scientific progress, because they rest on what science hasn’t yet explained. Feser’s point is that his proofs have a completely different structure: they rest on what every scientific explanation must presuppose.
summary.plain: The “god of the gaps” charge says theists invoke God to explain whatever science hasn’t explained yet, and science keeps closing those gaps. Feser replies that his arguments aren’t about gaps at all. They start from facts that any scientific theory will always involve (things change, have parts, and could have been otherwise), so no scientific discovery can make them go away.
summary.takeaway: The proofs start from what every scientific explanation presupposes, so science can’t fill the “gap” they point to.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: metaphysical versus physical starting points.** Imagine that physics finally discovers the complete “theory of everything,” T. What will T describe? Some fundamental entities or fields, in states that could be otherwise, passing from one state to another. Those are potentials being actualized. The entities will have structure, whether parts or at least distinct features, so they will be composite. Their laws could have been different, so they will be contingent, with an essence distinct from their existence. Every one of the proofs’ starting points will be present in T’s world, just as it is in a kettle of water. So T won’t close the “gap.” It will give us a more precise picture of the very features the arguments start from.

Contrast a genuine gap argument: “We can’t explain lightning, so Zeus must throw it.” Once electrostatics explains lightning, Zeus is out of a job. Arguments like that are probabilistic (“God is the best current explanation”) and always open to replacement. The proofs claim something much stronger: that no non-divine explanation is possible *in principle* for their starting points. They could be wrong, as Feser acknowledges, but they would be wrong because a premise is false, not because a new experiment came in (step 10).

**Ockham’s razor, slowly.** The razor says not to multiply entities beyond necessity. It is a tie-breaker among explanations that each do the job. The proofs claim that the universe can’t do the job of ultimate explanation, so citing the razor assumes the point in dispute.

**Harris’s humility.** Saying that nobody knows how or why the universe came to be sounds modest. But it quietly treats the question as a scientific one that more data might answer, which is the same assumption.

**The usual confusion.** People treat any appeal to God in an explanation as god-of-the-gaps. The label fits only arguments that rest on ignorance, not arguments that rest on what we know about change, composition, and contingency. Behind the objection lies scientism, the view that only science yields knowledge, which Feser takes on directly in ch7b.

checks.q: According to Feser, what defines a god-of-the-gaps explanation?
options: Any explanation that mentions God
One on which a non-divine explanation might in principle be correct, with God claimed only as the more probable one
One that relies on revelation
One that concerns the Big Bang
checks.explanation: The defining feature is merely probabilistic support that further discovery could replace.

checks.q: Why can’t a future “theory of everything” close the gap the proofs point to?
options: Because physicists will never agree on one
Because such a theory would be too complex
Because it would itself describe things with potentials, structure, and contingent laws, which are the proofs’ starting points
Because God would prevent its discovery
checks.explanation: The proofs start from features that any physical theory presupposes rather than from gaps in one.

checks.q: What is wrong, on Feser’s view, with appealing to Ockham’s razor against the proofs?
options: Ockham’s razor has been refuted
Ockham was a theologian, so the razor favors God
The razor applies only to biology
It treats the proofs as rival hypotheses to be judged by simplicity, when they claim that no physical explanation could be ultimate at all
checks.explanation: Parsimony chooses among adequate explanations; it can’t settle whether the universe is an adequate ultimate explanation.

summary.heading: A “universe from nothing”
summary.body:
The **second** problem: the proposed scientific explanation is a nonstarter, because a law like gravity isn’t nothing.

Krauss’s book notoriously commits the same error; Feser notes harsh criticism even from philosophers with no theological stake, especially David Albert’s 2012 *New York Times* review. Of about 185 pages, the first 152 argue the universe arose from empty space with energy under physical law — admitted not to be nothing. By about page 170 Krauss pares this to the laws of quantum gravity — also admitted not to be nothing. At page 177 he suggests layer upon layer of laws.

How any of this is “from nothing” is never explained. Talk of candidates for nothingness and of nothing as physical treats nothing as an elusive stuff that is hard to measure. But nothing is no stuff at all — simply the absence of anything. Krauss himself concedes his candidates aren’t really nothing, and what remains, laws or layers of laws, is something that can’t be the ultimate explanation.

(The chapter goes on to scientism, laws of nature, the complexity of a designer, and further objections, covered in ch7b.)

**What the physics does and doesn’t show.** Nothing in Feser’s criticism disputes the physics. It may well be true that, given certain fields and laws, a universe like ours can emerge from a state physicists call a vacuum. That is a claim about how one physical state gives rise to another. The claim on the book cover, a universe from *nothing*, is about why there is any physical state or law at all. The first is an interesting scientific result; the second is a philosophical conclusion the science doesn’t reach.
summary.plain: Some physicists claim the universe could arise from “nothing.” Feser points out that their “nothing” always turns out to be something: empty space full of energy, or the laws of physics. Real nothing means no space, no energy, no laws, nothing at all, and the question of why any of those things exist is left untouched.
summary.takeaway: Any “universe from nothing” that begins with space, energy, or laws begins with something, and so leaves the real question untouched.
summary.deepDive:
**The hardest idea: why “nothing” isn’t a very empty physical state.** Start with a box full of marbles. Take out the marbles, and the box is empty of marbles but still contains air. Pump out the air, and now it contains no matter, but it still has space, quantum fields in their lowest-energy state, and the laws of physics governing what could happen there. According to quantum field theory, that “vacuum” can indeed produce particles. But notice that at every stage we were subtracting things *from* something. Nothing isn’t the box with everything removed. It is no box, no space, no fields, and no laws: not a state of anything at all.

That is why, by his own admission, each of Krauss’s “candidates for nothingness” fails:

1. Empty space with energy and laws is something.
2. The laws of quantum gravity alone are something.
3. Layers of laws are something, and now we are back to the hierarchy of step 8.

Treating nothing as a stuff that is hard to measure, or saying it must be defined empirically, gets things backwards. Nothing isn’t hard to define. It is the absence of anything.

**Hawking and Mlodinow.** Their claim that the universe can create itself from nothing *because there is a law like gravity* refutes itself: if there is a law like gravity, there isn’t nothing. And a law, as the three views of laws showed (step 7), can’t be the ultimate explanation anyway.

**How it feeds the formal argument.** This is equivocation on a key term (step 11) combined with treating laws as ultimate (step 7).

**Nuance.** Feser notes that the harshest criticism of Krauss came from philosophers with no religious stake, above all David Albert. So the dispute isn’t theists against science. It is about whether a book’s conclusion follows from its physics.

**The usual confusion.** “Physicists have a technical sense of ‘nothing.’” Fine, but then they have answered a different question from the one about why anything exists at all.

checks.q: Where does Krauss end up, according to Feser, after admitting that his earlier candidates aren’t nothing?
options: With the claim that God created the laws
With a pure vacuum containing no laws
With the conclusion that nothing is a measurable kind of stuff
With the suggestion that there may be layer upon layer of laws
checks.explanation: At page 177 he suggests layers of laws, which are still something and can’t be ultimate.

checks.q: What is the basic flaw in saying that, because there is a law like gravity, the universe can create itself from nothing?
options: A law like gravity is itself something, so the starting point isn’t nothing
Gravity is too weak to create a universe
The universe is too old
Laws can only be discovered, not used in explanation
checks.explanation: The explanation presupposes the existence of the law, so it isn’t an account of arising from nothing.

argument.name: The Misfire Diagnosis: why the popular objections fail to engage the arguments
argument.overview:
This part of chapter 7 is not a proof of God but a sustained *meta-argument*: a demonstration that the most common objections to First Cause reasoning never make contact with the arguments actually defended in chapters 1–6. Feser applies the same small set of diagnostic tests again and again. Learn the tests and you can take apart almost any popular objection on the spot.

The reasoning has three stages. **Stage 1** fixes what the arguments really claim — their premises, their principled criterion for what needs a cause, and the kind of regress they rule out. **Stage 2** runs the diagnostic tests: does the objection attack a premise nobody holds (straw man)? Does it ignore the principled criterion? Does it confuse a hierarchical (per se) series with a temporal (per accidens) one? Does it equivocate on key words such as “cause”, “necessary”, or “nothing”? Does it beg the question by assuming scientism or by appealing to something that itself needs explaining? Is it true but irrelevant? **Stage 3** draws the verdict: each objection in this module fails one or more tests, so the real debate must shift to the premises themselves — which is where a serious critic ought to have been all along.

In conversation, the pattern gives you a calm three-move reply: (1) restate what the argument actually says; (2) name which test the objection fails; (3) invite the objector to engage the real premise.

stages.title: Stage 1 — What the arguments actually claim
stages.gist: The proofs do not assume “everything has a cause” or a beginning of time; they identify a specific feature that makes things need a cause and argue for a first cause lacking that feature, at the head of a here-and-now hierarchical series.

stages.title: Stage 2 — The diagnostic tests
stages.gist: Each popular objection fails at least one test: straw man, ignoring the principled criterion, per se/per accidens confusion, equivocation, question-begging, or true-but-irrelevant.

stages.title: Stage 3 — The verdict
stages.gist: None of the common objections engages the arguments; the only live options for a critic are to attack the real premises or show the key concepts incoherent.

steps.text: An objection counts against an argument only if it targets the argument as its defenders actually state it, not a version no defender holds.
steps.why: This is simply the rule against straw men. Feser presses it through the Darwinism analogy: defining Darwinism as “a monkey once gave birth to a human” and then refuting that would be rightly scorned, even if called a “stepping-stone.” Every objection in this module is measured against this rule first.
steps.example: Refuting “a monkey gave birth to a human” refutes no Darwinian. Likewise, refuting “everything has a cause, so God exists” refutes no defender of the cosmological argument.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it fair to criticize the popular version of an argument, since that is what most people actually believe?
steps.answer: Criticizing a popular misunderstanding is fine, but it isn’t then a criticism of the argument Aristotle, Aquinas, or Leibniz gave, so the conclusion “the cosmological argument fails” doesn’t follow. Feser’s complaint is that critics present the caricature as the argument itself.

steps.text: The book’s arguments — and the historical cosmological arguments of Aristotle, Aquinas, Leibniz, and the rest — do not rest on the premise that everything has a cause; they do not assume the universe began; and most make no claim about the universe as a whole.
steps.why: Feser lists some thirty major defenders from Plato to Craig, none of whom offers the “basic cosmological argument”; Le Poidevin himself admits nobody has. Some defenders deny that everything has a cause. Only the kalām version even tries to prove a beginning. Applies to: “What caused God?”, the “basic cosmological argument”, “Why assume a beginning?”, and the fallacy-of-composition charge.
steps.example: Chapter 1 starts from a single cup of coffee existing here and now. It has no premise that everything has a cause, no claim about a beginning, and no claim about the universe as a whole.
steps.challenge: Maybe the defenders are implicitly committed to “everything has a cause,” even if they never state it.
steps.answer: Feser denies this. Some defenders explicitly or implicitly deny that everything has a cause, and their principles apply only to things with potentials, parts, a distinct essence and existence, or contingency. So no commitment to the universal premise can be read off their arguments.

steps.text: Each causal proof picks out a specific feature that makes a thing need a cause — having potentials actualized, being composite, having an essence distinct from its existence, or being contingent — and argues for a first cause that lacks that feature and so could not in principle have a cause.
steps.why: This is the “principled criterion”. It is why God’s being uncaused is not an arbitrary exception but the conclusion of the argument: pure actuality, absolute simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity are exactly the absence of what calls for a cause. Applies to: “What caused God?”, “Maybe the universe is the uncaused cause”, the ontological-argument objection.
steps.example: The water in the kettle needs the flame because its potential for heat can’t actualize itself. Pure actuality, having no potentials, needs nothing to actualize it.
steps.challenge: Isn’t “something that lacks the feature” just a convenient way of defining God as the exception?
steps.answer: No. The lack is derived, not stipulated. The proofs argue that a hierarchical series of things with the feature can terminate only in something without it, so uncausedness is the result of the argument, not an assumption smuggled into it.

steps.text: The regress the arguments rule out is a hierarchical (per se) series, in which each intermediate member has causal power only derivatively and here-and-now; they allow that a temporal (per accidens) series could in principle stretch back without a beginning.
steps.why: From chapter 1: the hand–stick–stone example, and the sticks and mirrors that need a source outside the series however long it is. Applies to: “Why assume a beginning?”, Krauss’s endless layers of laws, and the fallacy-of-composition charge.
steps.example: The hand moves the stick, which moves the stone, and the stick moves nothing unless the hand is acting now. By contrast, a grandfather can die and his grandson can still have children.
steps.challenge: Why can’t a hierarchical series simply go on forever, as a temporal one might?
steps.answer: Because its members have only derived power. However many there are, none has the power in itself, so without an underived source nothing in the series would act at all (chapter 1).

steps.text: Therefore objections that attribute “everything has a cause” or a temporal beginning to the arguments attack a straw man and have no force against them.
steps.why: Follows from 1 and 2. This disposes of “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”, the claim that sophisticated versions are patches on the “basic” argument, and the multiverse reply insofar as it targets a beginning. The Hume–Russell genealogy (step 6) explains why the straw man is so widespread.
steps.example: “What caused God?” and “the argument assumes a beginning” both target premises that no defender uses.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t these objections still work against some version, such as the kalām argument?
steps.answer: The kalām argues for a beginning rather than assuming it, and even it doesn’t claim that everything whatsoever has a cause. In any case, the book’s arguments rely on neither premise, so the objections leave them untouched.

steps.text: The straw man arose historically from a confusion between a cause in the sense of a sufficient reason (which rationalists said everything has, God included) and a cause in the sense of an efficient cause distinct from its effect (which no theist says God has).
steps.why: W. Norris Clarke’s diagnosis: Descartes and Spinoza spoke of God as “self-caused”, meaning roughly that God explains himself; Hume merged the two senses and pinned the result on cosmological arguers generally; Russell, the Mills, and textbook writers such as Hospers passed it on. This supports step 5 and dissolves the claim that some theists really did hold the premise.
steps.example: Descartes called God self-caused, meaning self-explanatory. Hume read “cause” as an outside producer, and then found theists contradicting themselves.
steps.challenge: Isn’t this just a speculative story about how Hume went wrong?
steps.answer: It rests on evidence Clarke gathered: Descartes’ preservation argument, the rationalists’ use of “cause” for sufficient reason, and the absence of any cited theist who used the premise. And the refutation of the objection doesn’t depend on the story; the story only explains the objection’s popularity.

steps.text: Objections that nominate a rival terminus — the universe, the Big Bang, a multiverse, quantum events, the laws of physics — fail because each candidate has the very feature (potentiality, composition, essence–existence distinction, contingency) that the principled criterion says requires a cause.
steps.why: Follows from 3. The objection merely suggests an alternative stopping point without showing it meets the criterion; that ignores the argument rather than answering it. Laws in particular are either descriptions (explaining nothing), Platonic entities (needing participation explained), or summaries of how substances behave (dependent on the substances). And if the universe did qualify, the result would be pantheism, not atheism.
steps.example: The Big Bang was a potential being actualized, the laws of physics could have been different, and a multiverse is composite. So each has what calls for a cause.
steps.challenge: Why not simply say the universe is necessary, just as God is claimed to be?
steps.answer: Then one must show that a changing, composite thing with contingent laws exists necessarily, which conflicts with each proof’s criterion. And even if that worked, Feser notes, the result would be pantheism, not atheism.

steps.text: Objections that treat the universe’s history or an endless stack of laws as removing the need for a first cause confuse a per accidens series with a per se series.
steps.why: Follows from 4. A beginningless multiverse would still need to be sustained in existence here and now; layers of laws in which each holds only as a special case of a deeper one form a hierarchical series, which must have a first member that imparts causal power without deriving it.
steps.example: A beginningless series of universes would still need to be sustained now. And layers of laws, each holding only as a special case of a deeper one, form a hierarchy like hand, stick, and stone.
steps.challenge: Doesn’t the multiverse at least remove the need for a cause of the Big Bang?
steps.answer: Perhaps of the Big Bang considered as an event in time, but the proofs never needed that. They ask what keeps the whole multiverse existing and acting at every moment, and why it exists at all.

steps.text: Objections that deny causal or explanatory principles rely on equivocation or bad inference: chance and indeterminism are not uncausedness, and conceiving A without B does not show A can exist without B.
steps.why: Chance presupposes non-chance causes (the farmer and the treasure, the tumbling boulders); quantum physics at most rules out deterministic causes; the triangle/trilateral and man/height cases show conceivability-apart is not possibility-apart; Anscombe shows Hume’s scenario is underdescribed. Applies to Stenger, Dennett, Rosenberg, Grayling, and Hume.
steps.example: The farmer’s treasure shows that chance presupposes causes. The triangle and the trilateral show that conceiving things apart isn’t possibility apart. Anscombe’s teleportation case shows that Hume’s scenario is underdescribed.
steps.challenge: Doesn’t quantum indeterminism at least show that the principle of causality isn’t strictly universal?
steps.answer: Only if the principle demanded deterministic causes, and it doesn’t. Quantum events still involve potentials being actualized within contingent quantum laws, which are themselves part of what needs explaining.

steps.text: Objections that appeal to science or brute fact beg the question: the arguments’ starting points are metaphysical conditions that any empirical theory presupposes, the physics invoked (quantum laws, gravity, the multiverse) is itself among what needs explaining, and refusing an explanation only here is special pleading.
steps.why: Applies to the god-of-the-gaps charge (Hitchens, Dawkins, Harris), Krauss and Hawking–Mlodinow on “nothing”, the quantum objection, and “maybe there’s no explanation in this case” (answered with Gerson’s point that the argument has already offered one). A strict metaphysical demonstration is not a probabilistic hypothesis and isn’t judged by parsimony.
steps.example: Hitchens’ appeal to Ockham’s razor treats God as a rival hypothesis to physics. But Feser’s proofs start from change and contingency, which any physics presupposes.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it arrogant for philosophy to claim knowledge that science can’t overturn?
steps.answer: The claim isn’t that philosophy trumps science. It is that any empirical theory takes certain things for granted (the actualization of potential, composite and contingent things), and the proofs reason about those. Whether their premises are true is argued in chapters 1–5, not assumed.

steps.text: Objections that misread technical terms, or that are true but irrelevant, do not touch the conclusion: “necessary” in the arguments does not mean “true by definition”, “nothing” means the absence of anything, and failing to prove the Trinity does not show that atheism is true.
steps.why: Kant’s and Grayling’s ontological-argument charge assumes necessity must be logical/definitional or merely conditional — a false dichotomy given the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, and Thomistic accounts of metaphysical necessity. Krauss treats nothing as a hard-to-measure stuff. The Trinity objection is compatible with the arguments succeeding. And the attributes objection simply overlooks the hundreds of pages of argument for the divine attributes (Aquinas, Samuel Clarke, chapter 6).
steps.example: Kant reads “necessary being” as “exists by definition,” and Krauss reads “nothing” as empty space. The Trinity objection is true, but it doesn’t bear on whether God exists.
steps.challenge: Isn’t “metaphysical necessity” just a vague label invented to escape Kant?
steps.answer: Feser gives it precise content in three ways: no potentiality, no composition, and essence identical with existence. Each explains why such a being could not fail to exist, so the label is neither vague nor ad hoc.

steps.text: Therefore every common objection considered in this part of chapter 7 misfires: none engages the arguments as actually stated and defended.
steps.why: Follows from 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 — each objection falls under at least one of the diagnostic failures.
steps.example: Every objection in this module can be sorted under at least one diagnostic failure. For example, “What caused God?” fails as a straw man, and “god of the gaps” fails by begging the question.
steps.challenge: Might there be popular objections not on this list that do succeed?
steps.answer: The chapter continues in ch7b with scientism, evil, divine hiddenness, and others, and Feser argues those fail too. The diagnosis here covers only the objections considered in this half of the chapter.

steps.text: A genuine critic remains free to argue that the arguments’ premises are false or that notions such as pure actuality, absolute simplicity, or subsistent existence are covertly incoherent.
steps.why: Feser explicitly grants this: the atheist may doubt the arguments succeed or try to expose hidden incoherence. That is a legitimate line of attack — but it requires grappling with the details rather than a one-line retort.
steps.example: Arguing that a purely actual being couldn’t know or will anything would be a genuine objection, and chapter 6 addresses worries of that kind.
steps.challenge: If a real objection is possible, isn’t Feser’s confidence overstated?
steps.answer: His confidence is that the common objections fail. He explicitly leaves room for a critic who engages the premises, and he claims only that he has answered such critics elsewhere in the book.

steps.text: So the popular objections leave the arguments standing, and the burden returns to the critic to engage their real premises and details; a single smug question cannot substitute for that work.
steps.why: Follows from 12 and 13. This is the practical upshot for persuasion: answer the misfire briefly, then move the conversation to the real premises (act and potency, composition, essence and existence, contingency), where the substantive debate belongs.
steps.example: In conversation, answer “What caused God?” in one sentence, then ask, “Does the universe have potentials that are being actualized right now?”
steps.challenge: Doesn’t shifting the burden to the critic just avoid defending the arguments?
steps.answer: No. The arguments are defended at length in chapters 1–6. The point here is that an objection has to engage that defense rather than a caricature of it.

keyTerms.definition: A distorted version of an opponent’s argument, attacked in place of the real one.
keyTerms.example: Refuting “everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause” when no defender of the cosmological argument ever argued that way.
keyTerms.origin: English idiom for a dummy opponent set up to be knocked down; in logic, the informal fallacy of refuting a misrepresented position.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simplification — a fair simplification keeps an argument’s premises in easier words; a straw man replaces them.

keyTerms.definition: Robin Le Poidevin’s label for the three-step argument: whatever exists has a cause; nothing causes itself; the universe exists; so the universe has an external cause. Le Poidevin admits no one has defended it.
keyTerms.example: Presented in textbooks as the core of the argument, with sophisticated versions treated as repairs to it.
keyTerms.origin: Robin Le Poidevin, *Arguing for Atheism* (1996), who admits no one has defended it.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The real cosmological arguments (Aristotle, Aquinas, Leibniz), which reason from change, composition, or contingency, never from “everything has a cause.”

keyTerms.definition: W. Norris Clarke’s name for the line of antitheistic argument (Hume, James and John Stuart Mill, Russell, mid-century textbooks like Hospers’) that keeps attacking the “everything has a cause” caricature without citing anyone who held it.
keyTerms.example: Russell’s lecture *Why I Am Not a Christian* taught the caricature and the stock reply to many later writers.
keyTerms.origin: W. Norris Clarke’s label (1970) for the line running from Hume’s *Dialogues* through James and J. S. Mill to Russell and mid-century textbooks.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Humean empiricism in general — Clarke’s label names only the habit of attacking the “everything has a cause” caricature.

keyTerms.definition: That which brings about or actualizes something else — in the traditional sense, something other than the effect it produces.
keyTerms.example: The builder is an efficient cause of the house. Theists deny that God has an efficient cause distinct from himself.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s “source of change”; Latin *causa efficiens*, literally “the making cause.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Sufficient reason — an explanation, which may lie in a thing’s own nature rather than in something distinct from it.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever accounts for why something exists or is as it is; a broader notion than efficient cause. All causes are explanations, but not all explanations are causes.
keyTerms.example: A necessary being is explained by its own nature, without being caused by anything.
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz’s *ratio sufficiens*, “sufficient reason.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Efficient cause — every cause explains, but some explanations (a necessary being’s own nature) are not causes.

keyTerms.definition: The principle, defended in chapter 5, that everything has an explanation — for contingent things, in something outside them; for a necessary being, in itself. Related forms: sufficient reason, explanation.
keyTerms.example: PSR-based arguments make no exception for God, so “What caused God?” cannot even get started against them.
keyTerms.origin: Named and championed by Leibniz (Latin *principium rationis sufficientis*); anticipated by Spinoza.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Principle of causality (PC) — PC concerns what actualizes a potential; PSR concerns the explanation of anything whatsoever.

keyTerms.definition: Descartes’ and Spinoza’s term for God, which Clarke reads as meaning roughly “self-explanatory” rather than “efficiently caused by himself.”
keyTerms.example: Descartes’ “preservation” argument implies everything has a cause — including God, who is self-caused — so it makes no exception for God.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *causa sui*, “cause of itself”; used of God by Descartes and Spinoza.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Self-creation (efficiently producing oneself), which is incoherent and which no Scholastic ascribes to God.

keyTerms.definition: Being with no potentiality whatsoever; the conclusion of the Aristotelian proof. What is purely actual has no potential that could be actualized, so it could not have a cause.
keyTerms.example: Asking what caused pure actuality is asking what actualized the potentials of that which has none.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *actus purus*, “pure act,” from Aristotle’s *energeia* via Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An extremely powerful being — pure actuality means having no potentiality at all, not merely a great deal of power.

keyTerms.definition: Having no parts of any kind; the conclusion of the Neo-Platonic proof. What has no parts needs nothing to combine them. Related forms: simple, divine simplicity, noncomposite.
keyTerms.example: The universe and any multiverse are composite, so they cannot be the absolutely simple first principle.
keyTerms.origin: Plotinus’s One; Latin *simplex*, “without fold, not compounded.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Simple” meaning easy to understand — divine simplicity means lacking parts, not being uncomplicated to grasp.

keyTerms.definition: The distinction between what a thing is and the fact that it is; central to the Thomistic proof. Where the two are distinct, something must join them; in God, essence just *is* existence.
keyTerms.example: The laws of physics could have been otherwise, which shows their essence is distinct from their existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *essentia* (from *esse*, “to be”) and *existentia*; the real distinction developed by Avicenna and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Concept vs. object — the distinction is within the thing itself (what it is vs. that it is), not between our idea and the thing.

keyTerms.definition: A contingent being could have failed to exist or been otherwise and needs an explanation outside itself; a necessary being could not have failed to exist and has its explanation in itself. Related forms: contingency, necessity, necessarily.
keyTerms.example: The universe, the Big Bang, and quantum events are all contingent.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *contingere*, “to happen, befall”; *necesse*, “unavoidable.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Temporary vs. everlasting — a thing could exist forever and still be contingent, because it depends on something else.

keyTerms.definition: Course term for the feature each proof identifies as what makes a thing need a cause (potentiality, composition, essence–existence distinction, contingency). It is what makes God’s being uncaused non-arbitrary.
keyTerms.example: It answers both “What caused God?” and “Why not stop at the universe?” at once.
keyTerms.origin: Course term summarizing Feser’s remark that the difference between God and everything else is in each case a principled one.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Stipulation — a stipulated exception is arbitrary; the criterion is derived from what makes things need causes.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each intermediate member has causal power only derivatively, here and now, from a member higher up; it must have a first member with underived power. Also called an essentially ordered series.
keyTerms.example: Layers of physical laws, each holding only as a special case of a deeper law.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *per se*, “through itself, essentially”; Scholastic terminology (Aquinas, Scotus).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A long temporal chain — a per se series concerns simultaneous dependence, not length or duration.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which earlier members produce later ones but need not continue acting; the proofs allow such a series might have no beginning. Also called an accidentally ordered series.
keyTerms.example: A beginningless sequence of universes in a multiverse — which would still need to be sustained in existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *per accidens*, “by way of what is incidental.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Accidental” meaning unintended — here it means an earlier cause isn’t needed for the later one to keep acting.

keyTerms.definition: Wrongly inferring that a whole has a property because its parts do. Not every part-to-whole inference is fallacious (chapter 5: red Lego bricks make a red object).
keyTerms.example: Grayling’s charge — but Feser shows the real fallacy is inferring that explaining each member explains the whole series.
keyTerms.origin: Traditional informal fallacy, catalogued since Aristotle’s *Sophistical Refutations*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Valid part-to-whole inference — some features (color, contingency) do carry over from parts to whole.

keyTerms.definition: An event arising from the unplanned intersection of independent causal lines; it presupposes non-chance causal regularities rather than excluding causality.
keyTerms.example: A farmer striking buried treasure while plowing.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s analysis in *Physics* II of chance as the coincidence of independent causal lines; the buried-treasure case is a stock example.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncaused — chance events have causes; what they lack is a single plan uniting the causal lines.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of a deterministic cause — a cause that necessitates exactly one outcome. Neither the principle of causality nor PSR requires determinism. Related forms: indeterministic, determinism, deterministic.
keyTerms.example: A quantum event that occurs probabilistically, but only given the contingent laws of quantum mechanics.
keyTerms.origin: Modern term, associated in physics with the standard interpretation of quantum mechanics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncausedness — an indeterministic cause still causes; it just doesn’t fix one outcome.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that since we can conceive of an effect without its cause, an uncaused event is possible.
keyTerms.example: Refuted by the triangle/trilateral and man/height cases and by Anscombe’s underdescription point.
keyTerms.origin: David Hume, *A Treatise of Human Nature* (1739), book I, part 3, section 3; repeated by A. C. Grayling.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Showing a concept is free of contradiction — Hume’s move rests on merely thinking of one thing without thinking of another.

keyTerms.definition: Anscombe’s objection that Hume’s imagined uncaused appearance doesn’t specify what makes it uncaused rather than caused unseen or teleported — and any specification brings causation back.
keyTerms.example: Distinguishing coming-into-being from being-transported requires a generating rather than a transporting cause.
keyTerms.origin: G. E. M. Anscombe’s essay on Hume’s argument that whatever begins to exist must have a cause (reprinted in her *Collected Philosophical Papers*, 1981).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Unfalsifiability — the problem is not that Hume’s scenario can’t be tested but that it doesn’t specify what it is supposed to show.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a standard everywhere except the one case where it is inconvenient.
keyTerms.example: Scientists never accept “maybe it has no cause” for a phenomenon they study — yet critics invoke it for the existence of the universe.
keyTerms.origin: Originally a legal term: pleading special circumstances to escape a general rule.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Principled exception — an exception is legitimate when a reason explains why the rule doesn’t apply.

keyTerms.definition: The necessity of a proposition true by definition or on pain of contradiction — the kind the ontological argument is usually taken to claim for God.
keyTerms.example: “A bachelor is unmarried.” The cosmological arguments do not claim God exists in this sense.
keyTerms.origin: Modern logic; related to Leibniz’s “truths of reason,” true on pain of contradiction.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysical necessity — grounded in a thing’s nature rather than the meanings of words.

keyTerms.definition: Being necessary only relative to something else — e.g., being a necessary condition for the world. Grayling says metaphysical necessity reduces to this.
keyTerms.example: Oxygen is necessary for fire; that doesn’t make oxygen something that couldn’t fail to exist.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic “necessity of supposition” (*necessitas ex suppositione*); Grayling’s “merely relative” conception.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Unconditional necessity — what cannot fail to be, whatever else is the case.

keyTerms.definition: Unconditional necessity grounded in a thing’s nature — pure actuality, absolute simplicity, or essence identical with existence — rather than in definitions of words.
keyTerms.example: What has no potential to lose existence, no parts to come apart, and no essence distinct from existence cannot fail to exist.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, and Thomistic traditions; contrasted with logical necessity in modern analytic philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical necessity — the cosmological arguments do not claim God’s existence follows from a definition.

keyTerms.definition: An appeal to God to fill a present gap in scientific knowledge, allowing that a natural explanation could in principle be correct and claiming only that the theistic one is more probable.
keyTerms.example: The book’s proofs are not of this kind: they are strict metaphysical demonstrations.
keyTerms.origin: Phrase associated with Henry Drummond (1890s) and C. A. Coulson (1950s), who warned believers against resting faith on gaps in science.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inference to an explanation as such — the fault of gap reasoning is resting on present ignorance, not explaining.

keyTerms.definition: An argument claiming to show that its conclusion is the only possible account of its starting point, judged by validity and truth of premises rather than by parsimony or empirical fit.
keyTerms.example: The claim that any actualization of potential ultimately requires a purely actual cause.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *apodeixis*, “demonstration”; Scholastic *demonstratio quia*, reasoning from effect to cause.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Empirical hypothesis — judged by fit with data and parsimony, and always revisable by new observation.

keyTerms.definition: Feser’s options: statements of regularity (describe, don’t explain), Platonic entities (require participation to be explained), or summaries of how substances behave by nature (dependent on substances). On none are laws ultimate explanations.
keyTerms.example: Hawking–Mlodinow’s appeal to “a law like gravity” inherits this problem.
keyTerms.origin: The regularity view descends from Hume; the Aristotelian “natures” view is defended by David Oderberg; Feser points to Stephen Mumford’s *Laws in Nature* for the debate.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Causes — on none of the views is a law itself a self-explaining source of existence.

keyTerms.definition: The sheer absence of anything whatsoever — not a kind of stuff, not empty space, not a quantum vacuum, not laws.
keyTerms.example: Krauss’s “candidates for nothingness” (space with energy, quantum gravity laws) are all something.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *nihil*; the ancient maxim *ex nihilo nihil fit*, “from nothing, nothing comes.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Quantum vacuum or empty space — a physical state with energy and laws, and therefore something.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God is identical with the world.
keyTerms.example: If the universe really were uncaused, self-explanatory, and necessary, the result would be pantheism, not atheism.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *pan* (“all”) + *theos* (“god”); the word dates from the early eighteenth century (John Toland).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Panentheism — the world is in God but God exceeds it; pantheism identifies God and world.

keyTerms.definition: The one version of the cosmological argument that tries to prove the universe had a temporal beginning.
keyTerms.example: Defended by William Lane Craig — but even he argues for, rather than assumes, a beginning.
keyTerms.origin: Arabic *kalām*, “speech,” the name of medieval Islamic dialectical theology (e.g., al-Ghazali); revived by William Lane Craig.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Aristotelian and Thomistic arguments — which do not require a beginning of time.

keyTerms.definition: The popular atheist writers of the 2000s–2010s whose objections this chapter targets: Harris, Dawkins, Dennett, Hitchens, Stenger, Krauss, Rosenberg, Grayling, and (on this topic) Hawking and Mlodinow.
keyTerms.example: Each repeats “What caused God?” or a variant.
keyTerms.origin: Label coined by journalist Gary Wolf in 2006 for Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, and others.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Atheist philosophers generally — many academic atheists are more careful, though Feser shows even some specialists repeat the caricature.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. It concerns only what passes from potency to act, not everything whatsoever.
keyTerms.example: Water becomes hot only because something actual, such as a flame, heats it.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle; the Scholastic maxim “whatever is moved is moved by another” (*quidquid movetur ab alio movetur*).
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Everything has a cause” — PC applies only to what has potential being actualized, so by its own terms it does not apply to pure actuality.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality is the way a thing actually is; potency (potentiality) is a real capacity to be otherwise. Change is the actualization of potency. Related forms: actual, actuality, actualize, actualization, potential, potentiality.
keyTerms.example: A rubber ball is actually round and potentially squashed; sitting on it actualizes that potential.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *energeia* and *dynamis*; Latin *actus* and *potentia*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Abstract possibility — a potency is a real capacity in an existing thing, not merely something logically possible.

keyTerms.definition: Any argument from some general feature of the world — change, composition, contingency, existence — to a first cause of that feature.
keyTerms.example: Aquinas’s first three Ways; Leibniz’s contingency argument; the book’s Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *kosmos*, “world”; the label “cosmological proof” comes from Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Design (teleological) argument — which reasons from order or purpose rather than from change or existence.

keyTerms.definition: Knowledge of God’s existence and nature attainable by reason alone, without appeal to revelation.
keyTerms.example: Chapter 7 defends natural theology as a whole against its common critics.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *theologia naturalis*; the term goes back to Varro, as reported by Augustine.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Revealed theology — knowledge of God from scripture or revelation, such as the doctrine of the Trinity.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that God exists derived from the concept of God alone. In Descartes’ version, existence is a perfection, so a supremely perfect being must exist.
keyTerms.example: Kant claims the cosmological argument secretly depends on it; Aquinas rejects it while accepting the cosmological argument.
keyTerms.origin: Anselm’s *Proslogion* (1078) and Descartes’ fifth Meditation; the name is Kant’s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Cosmological argument — which starts from facts about the world, not from a definition.

keyTerms.definition: The rule not to multiply entities beyond necessity: among rival explanations that each do the job, prefer the simpler.
keyTerms.example: Hitchens says positing God violates it; Dawkins thinks a physical singularity more economical.
keyTerms.origin: Named after William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), though the famous wording is later.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A disproof — the razor only chooses among adequate explanations; it cannot eliminate one that is argued to be the only possible one.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming, in the course of an argument, the very point in dispute.
keyTerms.example: Insisting that only science can explain, and so God can’t, assumes exactly what the cosmological argument denies.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *petitio principii*, “assuming the starting point.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Raising the question” — in everyday speech “begs the question” often means “prompts a question”; in logic it means circularity.

keyTerms.definition: A fact that has no explanation at all, not even in principle.
keyTerms.example: “Maybe there’s no explanation in this case” treats the existence of the universe as a brute fact.
keyTerms.origin: Modern analytic philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A fact not yet explained — something whose explanation we don’t know is not thereby brute.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that, given its circumstances, fixes exactly one outcome.
keyTerms.example: A billiard ball struck at a given speed and angle travels to one predictable spot.
keyTerms.origin: Modern term, associated with Laplace’s picture of a fully predictable universe.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Cause as such — a cause can be probabilistic without ceasing to be a cause.

keyTerms.definition: God’s continual causal action keeping things in existence at every moment. Feser argues even a beginningless universe or multiverse would need it.
keyTerms.example: Like light that shines only while the current flows, not like a house that stands after its builder leaves.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic *conservatio*; central to Descartes’ preservation argument; developed in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Creation at a first moment — conservation concerns every moment, whether or not there was a first one.

keyTerms.definition: The Thomistic description of God: a being whose essence just is existence, rather than a thing that has existence added to it.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s footnote: say God’s essence *is* existence, not that it “includes” existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *ipsum esse subsistens* (Aquinas).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A being that has existence as one property among others — which would imply composition.

keyTerms.definition: A series of causes or explanations with no first member.
keyTerms.example: Krauss’s suggestion that there may be layer upon layer of physical laws without end.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *regressus in infinitum*; *ad infinitum*, “to infinity.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: An infinite past — the proofs allow a beginningless per accidens series but not a per se series without a first member.

keyTerms.definition: The hypothesis that our universe is one of many, possibly within a beginningless series of branching universes.
keyTerms.example: Rosenberg and Krauss propose that our Big Bang branched off from a preexisting universe.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary cosmology (inflationary and related models).
keyTerms.confuseWith: “Everything that exists” — a multiverse is still a composite, contingent physical system with potentials being actualized.

keyTerms.definition: The view that science is the only genuine source of knowledge, so any serious explanation must be scientific.
keyTerms.example: It underlies the god-of-the-gaps charge; Feser examines it directly at the start of the chapter’s second half (ch7b).
keyTerms.origin: “Science” + “-ism”; a critical label since the early twentieth century.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Respect for science — one can value science fully while denying it is the only form of knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: A proposed explanation tested by observation and judged by predictive success, parsimony, and fit with established theory.
keyTerms.example: A model of the early universe beginning from a singularity.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *empeiria*, “experience.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysical demonstration — which claims to show what any empirical theory must presuppose.

keyTerms.definition: In Platonism, the relation by which a concrete thing has a feature by sharing in an abstract Form.
keyTerms.example: If laws of nature were Platonic entities, the world would have to participate in them — and we would need to explain why it participates in these laws rather than others.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *methexis* (Plato); Latin *participatio*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere description — a law that only describes regularities involves no participation, and explains nothing.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional conception of God as one, simple, immutable, eternal, immaterial, omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good cause of all things.
keyTerms.example: Aquinas spends roughly a hundred double-column pages of the *Summa Theologiae* deriving these attributes right after the Five Ways.
keyTerms.origin: The shared view of Augustine, Anselm, Maimonides, Avicenna, Aquinas, and others.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The doctrines of a specific religion (Trinity, Incarnation) — which the arguments do not claim to prove.

keyTerms.definition: Course term for an objection that never makes contact with the argument it targets, because it attacks a straw man, ignores the argument’s stated principle, confuses two kinds of causal series, equivocates, begs the question, or is true but irrelevant.
keyTerms.example: “If everything has a cause, what caused God?” misfires because no defender uses the premise it attacks.
keyTerms.origin: Course label summarizing the pattern of Feser’s replies in chapter 7.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A refuted objection that engages the premises. Such an objection is a genuine challenge that happens to fail; a misfire never reaches the argument at all.

keyTerms.definition: Chapter 1’s argument from change: change is the actualization of potential, which requires something already actual, and a hierarchical series of actualizers must terminate in a purely actual actualizer (Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover).
keyTerms.example: The kettle’s water heated by the flame, whose activity depends here and now on deeper causes, up to pure actuality.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle (*Physics* book 8, *Metaphysics* book 12), developed by Maimonides and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A temporal “first mover” argument. The proof concerns present, hierarchical dependence, not the first event in time.

keyTerms.definition: Chapter 2’s argument from composition: anything made of parts needs a cause of the parts’ being combined, so there must be an absolutely simple, noncomposite first principle (Plotinus’s One).
keyTerms.example: The universe and any multiverse are composite, so neither can be the uncaused first principle.
keyTerms.origin: Plotinus and the Neo-Platonic tradition.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Augustinian proof, which argues from abstract objects to a divine intellect rather than from composition.

keyTerms.definition: Chapter 3’s argument from abstract objects such as numbers, propositions, and universals to a divine intellect in which they exist. Feser notes that it is not a causal argument, so “What caused God?” isn’t even superficially relevant to it.
keyTerms.example: Mathematical truths that are necessary and eternal are argued to require an eternal, necessary mind.
keyTerms.origin: Augustine, drawing on Platonism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The cosmological (causal) proofs, which reason from change, composition, essence and existence, or contingency.

keyTerms.definition: Chapter 4’s argument from the distinction between essence and existence: whatever has an essence distinct from its existence must have existence imparted to it, ultimately by something whose essence just is existence.
keyTerms.example: The laws of physics could have been otherwise, which shows that their essence is distinct from their existence, so they cannot be the uncaused cause.
keyTerms.origin: Thomas Aquinas, especially *De ente et essentia*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aquinas’s Five Ways, a different set of arguments. The Thomistic proof in this book is based on the essence–existence distinction.

keyTerms.definition: Chapter 5’s argument from the principle of sufficient reason: contingent things, and the collection of them, must have an explanation, which can ultimately lie only in a necessary being.
keyTerms.example: Leibniz’s infinitely copied geometry books leave the series’ content unexplained without such a being.
keyTerms.origin: Leibniz and the early modern rationalists; Samuel Clarke.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ontological argument. The rationalist proof starts from existing contingent things, not from a definition of God.

keyTerms.definition: Something that causes without itself being caused. In the proofs, it is something that *could not* be caused, because it lacks the feature (potentiality, composition, essence distinct from existence, contingency) that makes things need causes.
keyTerms.example: Pure actuality actualizes other things but has no potentials that anything could actualize.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s “unmoved mover”; the Scholastic *causa prima non causata*.
keyTerms.confuseWith: “A cause that happens to have no cause,” as in brute-fact views. The proofs’ uncaused cause is uncaused necessarily, by its nature.

keyTerms.definition: Treating something as belonging to a kind it doesn’t belong to, and so asking questions about it that make no sense for things of its real kind.
keyTerms.example: Asking what actualized the potentials of pure actuality, like asking for the name of a bachelor’s wife.
keyTerms.origin: Term popularized by Gilbert Ryle (1949).
keyTerms.confuseWith: An unanswered question. A category mistake is malformed, not merely unanswered.

keyTerms.definition: The movement arguing that certain biological structures are best explained by an intelligent designer rather than by natural selection. Feser uses it only in an analogy.
keyTerms.example: Feser imagines ID theorists defining “basic Darwinism” as a monkey giving birth to a human.
keyTerms.origin: A late-twentieth-century movement (e.g., Behe, Dembski).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The cosmological arguments, which do not argue from biological complexity at all.

keyTerms.definition: Descartes’ argument in the third Meditation that something must preserve him in existence from moment to moment. It implies a sense in which everything, including a self-caused God, has a cause.
keyTerms.example: Clarke shows that even this argument escapes “What caused God?”, since it makes no exception for God.
keyTerms.origin: René Descartes, *Meditations on First Philosophy* (1641), Meditation III.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Descartes’ ontological argument in Meditation V, which reasons from the idea of a supremely perfect being.

keyTerms.definition: The seventeenth- and eighteenth-century school (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz) that emphasized reason and principles such as the principle of sufficient reason as sources of knowledge. Its members are rationalists.
keyTerms.example: Descartes and Spinoza spoke of God as “self-caused,” meaning self-explanatory.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *ratio*, “reason”; the label distinguishes them from the empiricists (Locke, Berkeley, Hume).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being “rational” in the everyday sense. Rationalism is a specific historical position about the sources of knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: Using a word in two different senses within one argument, so that the argument appears valid when it isn’t. The adjective is “equivocal.”
keyTerms.example: Hume’s slide between “cause” as sufficient reason and “cause” as an efficient cause distinct from its effect.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *aequivocus*, “of equal voice,” meaning one word with several meanings.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Ambiguity in general. Equivocation is the fallacy of exploiting an ambiguity inside an argument.

keyTerms.definition: The medieval and later tradition of systematic philosophy and theology, centered on Aristotle and figures such as Aquinas and Scotus. Its adherents are Scholastics, and its terms (per se, actus purus, and so on) appear throughout the book.
keyTerms.example: Clarke calls the Hume–Russell target a hybrid that neither Scholastics nor Cartesians would recognize.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *scholasticus*, “belonging to the schools” (the medieval universities).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere hair-splitting, a popular caricature. Scholasticism is a body of worked-out philosophical positions and methods.

keyTerms.definition: Being made up of parts, whether physical parts or metaphysical ones such as essence and existence. A composite thing needs something to account for its parts being combined; what is noncomposite is simple.
keyTerms.example: A multiverse is composite, so on the Neo-Platonic criterion it needs a cause.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *compositio*, “putting together.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: The fallacy of composition, a logical error about part-to-whole inference, which is a different topic.

keyTerms.definition: The point at which a chain of causes or explanations ends, because something is reached that needs no further cause or explanation.
keyTerms.example: The skeptic proposes the universe as the terminus; the proofs argue that only something purely actual, simple, and necessary can be one.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *terminus*, “boundary, end.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: An arbitrary stopping place. A genuine terminus is something that by its nature could not have a further cause.

keyTerms.definition: The cosmological model on which the observable universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense early state about 13.8 billion years ago. The phrase “Big Bang singularity” refers to the model’s idealized starting point.
keyTerms.example: Feser says the Big Bang involved the actualization of a potential, so it can’t be an uncaused cause.
keyTerms.origin: The term was coined by Fred Hoyle (1949); the model was developed by Lemaître and others.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The beginning of time proved philosophically. The book’s arguments don’t depend on whether the Big Bang was an absolute beginning.

keyTerms.definition: The physical theory of matter and energy at the smallest scales, on whose standard interpretation some events (such as radioactive decay) are indeterministic, with only their probabilities fixed.
keyTerms.example: Dennett and Rosenberg cite quantum mechanics to argue that events can occur without causes.
keyTerms.origin: Developed in the 1920s by Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Bohr, and others.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A proof of uncaused events. At most it shows that some causes are not deterministic.

keyTerms.definition: In physics, the lowest-energy state of quantum fields, which still contains fields, energy, and laws and can give rise to particles. It is often loosely called “nothing.”
keyTerms.example: Krauss’s first candidate for nothingness, empty space endowed with energy and governed by law, is of this kind.
keyTerms.origin: Quantum field theory.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Nothing. A vacuum is a physical state; nothing is the absence of any state at all.

keyTerms.definition: The thing that needs to be explained, as opposed to the explanans, the thing that does the explaining.
keyTerms.example: A law understood as a mere statement of regularity just redescribes the explanandum.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “that which is to be explained.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Explanans, the explanation offered for the explanandum.

keyTerms.definition: Being all-powerful: able to bring about anything that is intrinsically possible. The adjective is “omnipotent.”
keyTerms.example: Dawkins claims there is no reason to call a first cause omnipotent; chapter 6 argues otherwise.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *omnis*, “all,” and *potens*, “powerful.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being able to do the logically impossible, such as making a square circle, which classical theists don’t mean.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing everything that can be known. The adjective is “omniscient.”
keyTerms.example: Aquinas and Samuel Clarke both argue that the first cause must have knowledge or intelligence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *omnis*, “all,” and *scientia*, “knowledge.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Knowing by observation or inference as humans do. Classical theism holds that God knows by knowing himself as the cause of all things.

keyTerms.definition: Changelessness: having no potential that could be actualized, and so undergoing no real change. The adjective is “immutable.”
keyTerms.example: Chapter 6: since change is the actualization of potential and God is pure actuality, God cannot change.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *in-*, “not,” and *mutabilis*, “changeable.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness or inactivity. An immutable God is supremely active, just not in a way that involves passing from potency to act.

keyTerms.definition: Existing without beginning, end, or succession, that is, outside time. It follows from immutability, since time is bound up with change. The adjective is “eternal.”
keyTerms.example: Feser’s list of divine attributes includes eternity alongside immutability and immateriality.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *aeternitas*; Boethius defined it as the complete possession all at once of unending life.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness, meaning existing through endless time. Divine eternity means being outside time altogether.

keyTerms.definition: Not being made of matter. Since matter always involves potentiality, what is purely actual cannot be material. The adjective is “immaterial.”
keyTerms.example: The arguments conclude to a first cause that is immaterial as well as eternal and immutable.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *in-*, “not,” and *materia*, “matter.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being ghostly or made of some subtle stuff. Immaterial means not being stuff at all.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of being one and unique: there is, and can be, only one God. Two purely actual beings would have to differ in some respect, which would imply potentiality in at least one of them.
keyTerms.example: This answers the follow-up question “Why not many first causes?”
keyTerms.origin: Chapter 6 (ch6a); classical theism generally.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere numerical oneness that happens to be the case. Divine unity is claimed to be necessary.

keyTerms.definition: The attribute of lacking no perfection. In the classical view, goodness is tied to actuality and badness to privation, so what is purely actual is perfectly good.
keyTerms.example: Included in the attributes that Aquinas and Samuel Clarke derive, and discussed in ch6b.
keyTerms.origin: The classical and Scholastic tradition (Augustine, Aquinas).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral goodness in the sense of obeying duties, which applies to creatures under a moral law rather than to God.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’s five brief arguments for God’s existence in the *Summa Theologiae* (part I, question 2, article 3): from motion, efficient causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and final causality.
keyTerms.example: Feser notes that Aquinas follows the Five Ways with about a hundred pages deriving the divine attributes.
keyTerms.origin: Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* (1265–1274).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The five proofs of Feser’s book, which differ in selection and development.

keyTerms.definition: Theism is belief in God; atheism is the denial that God exists. Classical theism is the specific traditional conception of God that the book defends.
keyTerms.example: Feser argues that a successful First Cause argument makes atheism false, leaving only the question of which theism is right.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *theos*, “god,” with the prefix *a-*, “without.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Agnosticism, which neither affirms nor denies God’s existence.

keyTerms.definition: Belief in God grounded purely in philosophical argument and not tied to any particular revealed religion.
keyTerms.example: Feser lists it alongside Judaism, Christianity, and Islam as an option once atheism is ruled out.
keyTerms.origin: Associated with thinkers such as Aristotle and, in the modern era, those who accept natural but not revealed theology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Deism, which adds the specific claim that God does not act in or sustain the world.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God made the world but does not sustain it or act in it thereafter. Chapter 6 argues against it by showing that God must conserve the world in existence at every moment.
keyTerms.example: Picturing God as a watchmaker who wound the universe up and walked away.
keyTerms.origin: Latin *deus*, “god”; associated with seventeenth- and eighteenth-century English and French thinkers.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Philosophical theism, which need not deny divine conservation or providence.

keyTerms.definition: The view that the world exists in God while God also exceeds the world. Chapter 6 argues against it along with pantheism.
keyTerms.example: Contrasted with pantheism, which simply identifies God with the world.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *pan*, “all,” *en*, “in,” and *theos*, “god”; coined by K. C. F. Krause in the nineteenth century.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Pantheism, which says the world *is* God rather than that it is *in* God.

keyTerms.definition: The reasoned defense of a religious faith. Natural theology can serve apologetics, but its arguments stand or fall as philosophy.
keyTerms.example: Feser’s book establishes the existence and nature of God but deliberately stops short of arguing for a particular religion.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *apologia*, “speech in defense.”
keyTerms.confuseWith: Apologizing in the sense of expressing regret.

keyTerms.definition: Presenting two options as the only possibilities when there is at least one more.
keyTerms.example: Grayling’s choice between logical and merely conditional necessity leaves out metaphysical necessity grounded in a thing’s nature.
keyTerms.origin: Also called a false dilemma; a traditional informal fallacy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A genuine dilemma, in which the two options really are exhaustive.

keyTerms.definition: Introduced just to rescue a position from an objection, without independent reason.
keyTerms.example: The skeptic suspects that God’s uncausedness is an ad hoc exception; Feser shows it follows from a principle.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, “for this (purpose).”
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled exception, which has an independent rationale explaining why the rule doesn’t apply.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term (such as “good,” “wise,” or “knows”) to God and creatures in senses that are neither exactly the same (univocal) nor completely different (equivocal), but related by proportion.
keyTerms.example: God’s knowledge is called knowledge by analogy with ours, though it lacks the composite structure human knowing has.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas’s doctrine of analogy, discussed in chapter 6.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphor. Analogical terms apply literally, though not in exactly the same way.

keyTerms.definition: Suspending judgment on whether God exists, often on the ground that the question cannot be settled.
keyTerms.example: Harris’s claim that nobody knows how or why the universe came into being has an agnostic flavor.
keyTerms.origin: Greek *a-*, “without,” and *gnosis*, “knowledge”; coined by T. H. Huxley (1869).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Atheism, which denies that God exists.

distinctions.name: Cause vs. sufficient reason (explanation)

left.label: Efficient cause
left.desc: Something distinct from the effect that brings it about or actualizes a potential in it. Traditional theists deny God has one.

right.label: Sufficient reason
right.desc: Whatever accounts for a thing’s existence or nature — possibly its own nature. Rationalists say everything, including God, has one.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Clarke traces the whole “What caused God?” tradition to Hume’s fusing of these: he took “everything has a sufficient reason” (Descartes, Spinoza) to mean “everything has an efficient cause distinct from itself”, then accused theists of contradicting it. Keep them apart and the supposed contradiction vanishes.

distinctions.name: Per se vs. per accidens causal series

left.label: Per accidens (temporal, linear)
left.desc: Earlier causes produce later effects and can drop out of existence; a beginningless series of this kind is not ruled out by the proofs.

right.label: Per se (hierarchical, here-and-now)
right.desc: Each member acts only by power derived simultaneously from a higher member; the series must have a first member with underived power, however many members it has.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Objections about a beginningless multiverse, “why must the regress end?”, and Krauss’s endless layers of laws all assume the proofs concern a temporal chain. The proofs concern the hierarchical kind — and layers of laws would themselves be hierarchical.

distinctions.name: Logical vs. conditional vs. metaphysical necessity

left.label: Logical / merely conditional
left.desc: Logical: true by definition, like “bachelors are unmarried” (the ontological argument’s kind). Conditional: necessary only relative to something else, like a precondition.

right.label: Metaphysical (unconditional, real)
right.desc: Grounded in a thing’s nature: pure actuality has no potential not to exist; absolute simplicity has no parts to separate; subsistent existence needs nothing added.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Kant and Grayling assume the cosmological argument needs either definitional necessity (which would make it depend on the ontological argument) or merely conditional necessity (which would be too weak). Feser shows this is a false dichotomy.

distinctions.name: God-of-the-gaps hypothesis vs. metaphysical demonstration

left.label: God-of-the-gaps hypothesis
left.desc: Allows that a natural explanation might in principle be correct; claims only greater probability; lives or dies by parsimony and empirical fit; shrinks as science advances.

right.label: Metaphysical demonstration
right.desc: Claims no alternative is possible in principle; starts from features any physical theory must presuppose (change, composition, contingency); judged by validity and truth of premises.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The New Atheist charge — Ockham’s razor, “science will fill the gap” — only works against the left-hand column. The proofs are in the right-hand column, so the charge begs the question.

distinctions.name: Chance / indeterminism vs. uncausedness

left.label: Chance or indeterministic event
left.desc: Arises from intersecting causal lines (chance) or from a cause that doesn’t fix one outcome (indeterminism); always operates within contingent causal regularities or laws.

right.label: Uncaused event
right.desc: Something coming about with no cause at all — which neither chance nor quantum mechanics shows ever happens.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Stenger, Dennett, and Rosenberg treat the left column as evidence for the right. But the principle of causality and PSR require a cause or explanation, not a deterministic one.

distinctions.name: Conceiving A without B vs. A being possible without B

left.label: Conceiving apart
left.desc: Thinking of one thing without, at the same moment, thinking of another — a fact about our attention.

right.label: Possible apart
right.desc: The one thing actually being able to exist without the other — a fact about reality.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Hume’s argument slides from the left to the right. We can think of a triangle without thinking “three-sided” and of a man without thinking of his height, but neither can exist without the other.

distinctions.name: “Nothing” vs. physicists’ “nothing”

left.label: Nothing (strictly)
left.desc: The absence of anything at all: no space, energy, fields, laws, or potential.

right.label: Krauss’s candidates
right.desc: Empty space with energy governed by laws; the laws of quantum gravity; layers of laws. All of these are something.

distinctions.whyItMatters: A “universe from nothing” that starts from laws or fields has not explained existence; it has relocated the question to those laws, which cannot be ultimate.

illustrations.title: The monkey who gave birth to a human
illustrations.body:
Imagine Intelligent Design advocates defining “the basic Darwinian thesis” as the claim that, long ago, a monkey gave birth to a human baby. They cite no Darwinian who ever said this, even admit that no one holds it — and yet present it as a handy stepping-stone to the more sophisticated versions of Darwinism.

Darwinians would be furious, and rightly: the framing makes everything they actually say look like a desperate rescue of an absurd idea. Feser’s point is that this is precisely what the “basic cosmological argument” does to Aristotle, Aquinas, and Leibniz. Use this analogy with anyone who respects science: it makes the unfairness of the straw man instantly felt.

illustrations.title: The farmer and the buried treasure
illustrations.body:
A farmer plowing a field strikes a chest of buried treasure. That is a textbook chance event — nobody planned the discovery. But look at what makes it happen: the farmer’s decision to plow in that direction that day, and someone else’s earlier decision to bury treasure in exactly that spot. Chance is the *crossing* of two perfectly ordinary causal lines.

The lesson: chance doesn’t show that something can happen without a cause. It presupposes causes. Remove the causal lines and there is no chance event left to talk about.

illustrations.title: The boulder that hit the boulder
illustrations.body: After an earthquake, a tumbling boulder A shatters boulder B. That *this* boulder hit *that* one is chance. Yet it happens only because of regularities — plate tectonics, gravity, the solidity of rock. Feser uses the case alongside the farmer to show that the “chance” objection (Stenger) is aimed at a straw man: no defender of the cosmological argument ever denied that chance events occur.

illustrations.title: The triangle and the man’s height
illustrations.body:
You can think about what a triangle is without thinking, at that moment, of its being trilateral (three-sided). Does it follow that a triangle could exist without three sides? Obviously not. You can think of a man without thinking of how tall he is; no man could exist with no height whatever.

Hume’s argument has the same form: we can think of an effect without thinking of its cause, so (he concludes) an effect could exist without a cause. The examples show the inference is invalid — what our minds can separate, reality may not.

illustrations.title: Anscombe’s mysterious appearance
illustrations.body: Try to imagine a rabbit popping into existence on your desk with no cause. Now ask: what in your mental picture makes it a case of *uncaused coming-into-being*, rather than a rabbit produced by an *unseen* cause, or teleported in from somewhere else? Nothing in the picture settles it. To make it the scenario Hume needs, you would have to add something — but the natural way to tell coming-into-being from being-transported is that the one has a *generating* cause and the other a *transporting* cause. Causation sneaks right back in. (The rabbit is the course’s example; the argument is Anscombe’s, as reported by Feser.)

illustrations.title: Sticks, mirrors, and copied geometry books
illustrations.body:
Three examples, one lesson.

- **Sticks:** a chain of sticks, each pushed by the next, even infinitely long, contains no stick that can move anything on its own — so the motion must come from outside the chain.
- **Mirrors:** an endless row of mirrors each reflecting a face from the next still requires an actual face somewhere outside the row.
- **Geometry books (Leibniz):** if each copy of a geometry text was copied from an earlier copy forever, you have a cause for each book but no explanation of why the series has *this* content at all.

Explaining each member by its neighbor does not explain the whole. So it is Hume and Grayling — not the theist — who commit the fallacy of composition when they claim nothing is left over.

illustrations.title: Relativity doesn’t explain evolution
illustrations.body: Nobody concludes that special relativity is false because it tells us nothing about how living things evolved, or that quantum mechanics is wrong because it doesn’t answer every engineering question. A theory is judged by what it claims to establish. The First Cause arguments claim to establish that there is one, simple, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good cause of the world — not the Trinity or the inspiration of Scripture. Complaining that they don’t prove the latter is like faulting relativity for silence on biology.

illustrations.title: Krauss’s shrinking “nothing”
illustrations.body:
Picture a magician who promises to pull a rabbit out of an empty hat. First he shows you a hat containing a rabbit-shaped cloud of energy. “Not quite empty,” he admits. Then a hat containing only the *rules* for making rabbits. “Also not empty,” he admits. Finally he suggests there may be rules behind the rules behind the rules. At no point was the hat empty.
